Abstract: Understanding how animals move between behaviors is a central question in neuroethology, yet most segmentation methods first partition time into discrete states, leaving transitions as the unmodeled residue between them. We take the opposite view: in a suitable feature space, sustained behaviors are dense regions of the trajectory's density landscape, and transitions are the sparse corridors and loops that connect them. Because this structure is a property of the landscape's shape rather than of any particular coordinates, it can be read off directly with topology and should persist across feature spaces. We build this landscape from frame-by-frame trajectories, extract its discrete-Morse graph, and keep two kinds of structure: paths, the corridors a trajectory follows between dense behavioral regions, and cycles, closed routes whose entry and exit take different ways. Clustering these structures yields transitions directly, with no upstream state partition. On a rat behavior dataset across three feature spaces, including the latent space of a neural-network controller that imitates the animal in a physics simulator, the approach recovers transitions at coverage comparable to state-space and topological-clustering baselines, while carrying substantially more information about the transition identity, forming clusters at least as tight as the baselines', and matching annotated transitions with less reliance on time-warping. More broadly, the results show that behavioral transitions are a topological feature of a representation: recoverable from the shape of its trajectories, and consistent across distinct feature spaces.

Machine Learning.title: Uncertainty Aware Quality-Diversity Optimization For Offline Biological Sequence Design
Machine Learning.summary:
arXiv:2611.00716v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Designing sequences such as nucleic acids and proteins with desired properties is a fundamental challenge in biology. Due to the vast, discrete nature of sequence spaces and the high cost of experimental evaluation, offline computational sequence design plays a crucial role in proposing novel sequences before costly wet-lab validation. In practice, it is also essential that proposed designs are diverse to increase the likelihood of downstream experimental success. This motivates methods that balance performance, novelty, and diversity, whilst mitigating against uncertainty inherent to offline optimization. Quality-Diversity optimization (QD) can discover diverse, high-performing solutions, making it well suited to this problem, but its elitist nature makes reliable exploration under uncertainty challenging. To address this, we introduce Prior-guided Offline MAP-Elites (POME), an uncertainty-aware QD framework explicitly adapted to the offline regime. Our method leverages foundation models as priors to guide search toward biologically plausible regions and enable robust exploration under uncertainty. Across three sequence design tasks, POME consistently improves both performance and diversity over prior offline QD methods, and achieves the most reliable balance compared to offline MBO baselines, obtaining the best performance on two tasks and the second-best on the third, while maintaining high diversity and novelty.

Machine Learning.title: Learning hidden-state dynamics from unpaired snapshots with lift-project SDEs
Machine Learning.summary:
arXiv:2611.00742v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Many systems are observed only through unpaired snapshots, with population samples available at each time point but no correspondence between samples at different times. These snapshots determine the one-time distributions but leave the temporal coupling unspecified, requiring a modeling prior to connect successive times. We propose the lift-project stochastic differential equation (SDE), an autonomous SDE on the observed coordinate and a few hidden coordinates, trained only to match the snapshots. Most existing methods, including time-dependent SDEs, Schr\"odinger bridges and optimal transport, evolve the observed coordinate alone. For a scalar observation, the classical comparison theorem implies that all such models have non-negative lagged covariance, so on data whose lagged covariance turns negative, their error has a computable floor. The lift-project SDE is not bound by this floor. On two representative partially observed systems, the Duffing and pendulum oscillators, at comparable fit to the snapshots, the proposed method reduces the lagged-covariance error by factors of 2.4 and 6.6 relative to the strongest baseline and is the only model below the error floor; one hidden coordinate is already enough for such improvement. Furthermore, if a second experiment changes only the initial state of the hidden coordinate, no single model that evolves the observed coordinate alone can fit both experiments, whereas a single lift-project SDE can.

Machine Learning.title: PeptSol: A Translational Benchmark for Protected-Peptide Solubility in Drug Manufacturing
Machine Learning.summary:
arXiv:2611.00749v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Liquid-phase peptide synthesis (LPPS) offers a scalable route to peptide manufacturing, but route development still depends on empirical solvent screens because each protected intermediate must be soluble for reaction and recoverable for purification. The protecting groups, terminal modifications, and noncanonical residues that govern this behaviour are poorly represented in existing peptide property benchmarks, limiting the ability to develop and rigorously evaluate molecular representation models for LPPS-relevant prediction tasks. We introduce PeptSol, an open benchmark of 1388 hand-curated protected-peptide solubility measurements with chemistry-aware splits. The measurements span only 84 parent sequences and 101 protected structures, and 92.5% come from a single historical programme. Across seven frozen molecular encoders, the best macro-F1 is 0.843 on binary solubility for the historical subset under a peptide-held-out split; the harder three-class ordinal task reaches 0.614 in that cell. No foundation model consistently outperforms a baseline combining chemical fingerprints with explicit molecular descriptors, and model rankings vary across prediction tasks and data splits. The dataset, evaluation protocol, and baselines establish a standard for measuring progress on molecular representations for synthesis-aware peptide developability.
Machine Learning.comment: Comments: 15 pages, 1 figure, 19 tables. Accepted at the AI for Drug Discovery workshop, NeurIPS 2026

Machine Learning.title: The Tangled Web They Weave: Exploring Neural Representations with Directed Simplicial Complexes
Machine Learning.summary:
arXiv:2611.00786v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Understanding how artificial neural networks (ANNs) represent and combine features internally is a central challenge in mechanistic interpretability. Existing neural circuit-discovery methods represent neuron interactions as pairwise edges in a graph. But distributed neural representations consist of large groups of neurons that are inherently linked by higher-order causal dependencies: suppressing a subgroup of neurons in concert may shift the activation of other neurons in the feature representation. We propose a method to construct filtered directed simplicial complexes (DSCs) that give a topological representation of such dependencies, built from the activation profiles of an ANN on a given set of inputs. Our approach treats ANNs as structural causal models and uses counterfactual ablations to test for causal links between groups of internal neurons within specific input contexts. As a proof of concept, we apply the approach to a pair of small multilayer perceptron (MLP) architectures in a synthetic two-dimensional quadrant classification task. In these examples, DSCs recover the designed feature pathways and coordinated class transitions, and the complexes of trained networks are higher-dimensional than those of their handcrafted references. As validation, we compare our method with graph-based circuit-discovery baselines and find that their 1-skeletons agree within the relations that a weight graph can represent. These results support DSCs as context-dependent descriptions of multi-neuron computation and may thus provide a novel, orthogonal framework to study the phenomenon of distributed feature representations and polysemanticity.

Machine Learning.title: Tight Stochastic Sequential Covers for General VC Classes with Unknown i.i.d. Features
Machine Learning.summary:
arXiv:2611.00788v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: We study hybrid online learning with stochastic features and adversarial labels when the feature distribution is unknown. Prior work gave stochastic sequential covers of log-size $O(d\log^2 T)$ for a general VC class and logarithmic bounds only under stronger star-type structure. We show that finite VC dimension alone is enough: every binary class of VC dimension $d$ admits a distribution-blind exact cover with log-size $O(d\log T+\log(1/\delta))$, matching the worst-case $\Omega(d\log(T/d))$ dependence on the horizon. The key ingredient is a new local cube weight that counts Boolean subcubes incident to each realizable trace. Unlike the equal splits used in earlier constructions, we split mass unevenly according to these cube weights; a coordinate-deletion inequality shows that VC dimension controls the total cost of these splits. This yields, to our knowledge, the first tight $O((d+1)\log T)$ expected worst-case log-loss regret for general VC partitions with unknown i.i.d. features, and an exact polynomial-time implementation for planar affine halfspaces. We also show that the binary phenomenon does not extend from VC dimension to pseudo-dimension: a fixed pseudo-dimension-one sigmoid class requires $\Omega(\log^2 T)$ bits for uniform sequential approximation at accuracy $1/T$.

Machine Learning.title: Crop Mapping Evaluation under Sampling Bias
Machine Learning.summary:
arXiv:2611.00794v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Government agencies use crop maps to estimate production, monitor food security, and set agricultural policy. These crop maps are usually validated against field labels, but these labels are rarely a random sample of the area the map covers. Field teams tend to label parcels near roads and skip ones that are small or hard to reach, so performance measured on held-out labels mainly describes the places they visited. We call the difference between this reported performance and performance over the whole mapped region the deployment performance gap. To estimate performance over the whole region, we use a weighted form of prediction-powered inference (PPI). The classifier's predictions on unlabeled points across the region give a first estimate, and its errors on the labeled points correct that estimate, with more weight on labels from under-sampled conditions. We test this in five European regions where crop registers label every declared parcel, so the true performance is known. Simulating six documented collection practices there produces gaps of up to 0.20 macro-F1. On the collection rule that creates the largest gap in each region, 5 km block cross-validation still overestimates macro-F1 by as much as 0.18, while PPI with weights estimated from satellite embeddings reduces the largest error across regions to 0.07. Importance-weighted cross-validation with the same weights does almost as well, so most of the improvement comes from the weights themselves. We also apply the method to three Kenyan datasets that have no region-wide reference labels. For a roadside dataset collected with helmet-mounted cameras, the estimated macro-F1 falls from 0.93 under random cross-validation to 0.61, although the correction relies on a small number of heavily weighted labels. Our code is available at https://github.com/microsoft/pappi.

Machine Learning.title: Private Uniform Language Generation
Machine Learning.summary:
arXiv:2611.00797v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: We study uniform language generation under approximate differential privacy. Given a uniformly bounded number of distinct examples from an unknown target language, a generator must produce infinitely many new examples from that language with probability one while protecting the privacy of its input. We introduce a new combinatorial dimension termed the nested branching dimension and prove that a language class is privately uniformly generatable if and only if both its closure dimension and nested branching dimension are finite. Previous work characterizes non-private uniform generation by the finiteness of the closure dimension alone. Our results therefore identify an additional combinatorial obstruction imposed by privacy.

Machine Learning.title: Streaming Virtual Metrology via Lightweight Adaptation under Temporal Distribution Shifts
Machine Learning.summary:
arXiv:2611.00806v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Virtual metrology (VM) aims to estimate costly or delayed metrology variables from heterogeneous sensor signals and in-line measurements, and it acts as a critical component of semiconductor manufacturing. While recent data-driven models have improved VM accuracy, most are trained in batch settings and assume stationary data distributions. In practice, however, production environments evolve continuously due to equipment degradation, process adjustments, and maintenance events, making conventional batch-trained VM models difficult to maintain under temporal distribution shifts. In this work, we propose GRAPE (Global Regression with Adaptive Prediction Enhancement), a practical online learning framework for VM in evolving wafer-processing environments. GRAPE integrates a stable global predictor based on interpretable representations with two lightweight streaming adapters that correct feature-level and environment-level shifts through online updates. Experiments on two real-world semiconductor manufacturing datasets, including chronologically held-out blind-test streams, show that GRAPE improves robustness and generalization under real temporal drift compared with both conventional batch-learning methods and existing online learning baselines.

Machine Learning.title: HamFormer: A Hamiltonian Flow-based SE(3)-Transformer for Conformation Optimization
Machine Learning.summary:
arXiv:2611.00875v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: The Transformer architecture plays a central role in modern deep learning, and its SE(3)-equivariant variants have been widely applied to molecular conformation modeling and optimization. Given its importance, many methods attempt to interpret and improve the Transformer through the lens of dynamics. However, they mainly focus on a single attention head rather than the full Transformer architecture and seldom consider SE(3)-equivariance in their proposed models. In this study, we propose an improved SE(3)-Transformer architecture, called HamFormer, which revisits the design of SE(3)-Transformer through the lens of Hamiltonian flow. In particular, we define a parametrized Hamiltonian flow in the phase space of position and velocity, corresponding to optimizing an energy functional that combines an optimal transport-based potential with a damped momentum. The Lie-Trotter splitting framework of the Hamiltonian flow leads to the proposed HamFormer architecture, whose feedforward computation achieves the optimization step of the proposed energy functional. Furthermore, we combine HamFormer with Equivariant Graph Neural Network (EGNN), build a new model for molecular conformation optimization. Extensive experiments on molecular ground-state conformation prediction show that HamFormer provides a strong and physically interpretable surrogate for classic SE(3)-Transformer and generally outperforms state-of-the-art competitors.

Machine Learning.title: Foresight: Learning Twisted SMC for Rare Events from Reversed Relaxations
Machine Learning.summary:
arXiv:2611.00903v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: We consider the probability that a reversible Markov chain started in a set $A$ is in a rare set $B$ after a fixed horizon, a quantity often needed for many start laws, down to single states. Twisted sequential Monte Carlo (SMC) estimates such probabilities without bias, with small variance when its proposal and twist approximate the dynamics conditioned on reaching $B$, but these components are usually learned from forward simulations, which contain almost no successful paths when the event is rare. We introduce Foresight-SMC, which learns both components from the target side: under reversibility, relaxations started in $B$ that return to $A$ are, read backwards, exact samples of the conditioned paths, and their number is governed by the return probability rather than by the rare probability. Extending this reversal to the recorded propose--accept decisions of a Metropolis-adjusted sampler, we fit a controlled Langevin proposal with exact likelihood ratios by maximum likelihood, together with a classifier twist; the resulting estimator is unbiased for any start law. A variance analysis shows that resampling reduces the variance when the importance weights degenerate, as they do over long horizons. On an Allen--Cahn field, the learned proposal alone suffices, and one trained model is more accurate than splitting at equal cost. On alanine tripeptide, resampling with the learned twist is necessary, and Foresight-SMC needs less computation per query than adaptive multilevel splitting on localized start sets.

Machine Learning.title: Benchmarking Classical Machine Learning Models for Shading-Fault Detection in Rooftop Photovoltaic Systems Using Real Sensor Data
Machine Learning.summary:
arXiv:2611.00917v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Most published comparisons of machine-learning classifiers for photovoltaic (PV) fault detection are validated on simulated faults. We compare seven classical and ensemble-tree classifiers on the R\'eunion dataset, a 4 kW domestic rooftop plant on which shading faults were physically staged and logged. Readings within a staged episode are near-duplicates, so every train/test split is grouped by episode. A 20,800-row subsample that retains all 17 fault episodes was evaluated with three repeats of five-fold group-aware nested cross-validation, with synthetic minority oversampling (SMOTE) applied inside the training folds. Random Forest and XGBoost gave the highest mean accuracy (0.838 and 0.831) and Matthews correlation coefficient (MCC; 0.526 and 0.522). After Holm correction across the 21 pairwise Wilcoxon tests, only Random Forest's accuracy advantage over k-nearest neighbours and the multi-layer perceptron remained significant. Logistic Regression and the Decision Tree (accuracy 0.820) could be separated neither from the ensembles nor from the weakest models. SMOTE lowered binary MCC for six of the seven classifiers. Errors were concentrated in whole episodes: the Random Forest almost entirely missed four of the 17 fault episodes, including one of two uniform-shading and two of five intermittent-shading episodes. A post-hoc diagnostic shows that the no-fault rows were sampled over a wider range of times of day and output levels than the fault rows. Clock time alone reaches an MCC of 0.44, and PV-side voltage alone 0.72. The reported scores therefore reflect operating-condition differences as well as shading signatures. We release the pipeline and the diagnostics, and identify matched no-fault sampling as the step needed before the classifier ranking can be generalised.

Machine Learning.title: TreePIN$^{2}$: Tree-Prior Initialized Neural Networks
Machine Learning.summary:
arXiv:2611.00919v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Fitted decision trees provide predictive knowledge for neural network initialization. We present Tree-Prior Initialized Neural Networks (TreePIN$^{2}$), a method that translates split rules, decision paths and leaf predictions into initial network weights and biases for classification and regression. Sigmoid units encode split responses, hidden units combine them along decision paths, and leaf predictions initialize the output layer. We calibrate split softness using local training margins, sample support and impurity reduction, relating the initial responses to the data at each node. All weights and biases remain trainable, allowing gradient-based optimization to refine the transferred decisions and their combinations. Across six classification and six regression tasks with twenty paired seeds, TreePIN$^{2}$ improves mean initial and early validation performance over initialization baselines on most tasks. After fifty epochs, it achieves the best or tied-best mean validation performance among the six compared methods on ten tasks. Paired ablations show how split calibration and leaf-informed output initialization contribute to the starting predictor and its subsequent learning.

Machine Learning.title: What matters in classical machine learning for non-intrusive load monitoring? A factorial benchmark on REFIT with validation on unseen houses
Machine Learning.summary:
arXiv:2611.00920v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Published classical machine-learning results for appliance ON/OFF classification in nonintrusive load monitoring (NILM) range from F1-type scores of 0.53 to 0.98, and the sources of this spread have not been separated. This study separates them with a factorial benchmark on REFIT: seven models, two feature sets and four class-imbalance strategies for five appliances (270 fitted configurations), each evaluated by pooled nested cross-validation and on houses unseen during training, with robustness checks. An analysis of variance shows that the appliance explains 38% of the variance in F1, the feature set 13% and the model only 8%. Engineered rolling-window features raised the mean F1 score by 52% under both protocols. Other conclusions changed on unseen houses: the support-weighted F1 score of the best pooled configurations fell from 0.548 to 0.447, the differences between the models selected by pooled validation were no longer significant, and the benefit of class weighting over no correction rose from 32% to 69%. In a nested comparison, house-grouped selection on the training houses improved F1 on unseen houses for three of five appliances, by up to 0.110, and was within 0.007 for the other two. These findings held across four house partitions and without the solar-affected houses. A same-protocol convolutional network reached a weighted F1 score of 0.50, about 0.05 above the classical models (0.45) and far below the published deep-learning scores of 0.78 to 0.91, which were obtained under a different protocol. The results support low-cost appliance monitoring in buildings and yield a NILM reporting checklist.

Machine Learning.title: Solvable dynamics model of in-context learning
Machine Learning.summary:
arXiv:2611.00921v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Pretrained Transformer architectures display a surprising in-context learning ability without additional training. How the learning process guides the network to achieve this intriguing capability remains unsolved. In this study, we focus on a single-layer, single-head linear attention model, where empirical risk minimization is defined for learning. Given a finite amount of training examples, we determine the exact solution of network parameter dynamics, which is linked to the training error and generalization error, characterizing how memorization and generalization emerge from learning and how these transitions are related to curvatures of the empirical risk landscape. Furthermore, we calculate a data-dependent free energy, from which the training and generalization errors in the long-time limit of learning dynamics can be well predicted. Our work adds insights toward understanding the mechanism of in-context learning, especially from a learning dynamics perspective.

Machine Learning.title: MarkovTS: Pretrained State-Transition Representations for Zero-Shot Time Series Generation
Machine Learning.summary:
arXiv:2611.00941v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Across heterogeneous real-world domains, time-series generation supports simulation, model development, and data augmentation by generating sequences that preserve target-domain statistics and temporal dependencies when real observations are scarce or costly. However, existing methods predominantly address in-domain generation, limiting their reuse in unseen domains. We study reference-conditioned zero-shot time series generation: target domains are unseen during pretraining, generation uses a single target-domain reference sequence, and no model parameters are updated. MarkovTS characterizes sequence evolution through local morphologies and their ordered transitions at multiple temporal scales. Its pretrained encoder quantizes normalized time-series patches into multiscale morphological states with a state codebook, while a transition codebook encodes contextual transitions between adjacent intervals. These transferable state-transition representations condition a pretrained flow-matching model. At generation, the frozen model combines a reference-derived condition with independent Gaussian noise to produce stochastic samples that retain the reference's temporal organization. Across 12 unseen target datasets, MarkovTS outperforms strong baselines in most distributional comparisons and generates diverse, reference-consistent sequences. As downstream augmentation, its samples yield overall gains across forecasting, classification, and anomaly detection benchmarks and diverse model families. Our code is available at https://github.com/blisky-li/MarkovTS.

Machine Learning.title: HieraNTP: Structured Risk Representations for Time-Series Anomaly Detection via Hierarchical Next-Token Prediction
Machine Learning.summary:
arXiv:2611.00945v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Time-series anomaly detection commonly converts deviations from learned temporal regularities into anomaly scores. This practice can conflate violations of temporal regularity with task-specific anomaly judgments: the same deviation may be anomalous under one task definition and benign under another. Aggregating heterogeneous deviations into a single score before task-specific adaptation can obscure the evidence needed to distinguish these cases. We introduce HieraNTP, a Hierarchical Next-Token Prediction framework that separates self-supervised predictive modeling from task-specific risk interpretation. HieraNTP pretrains a hierarchical tokenizer and a causal next-token predictor to capture temporal regularities at multiple scales. It then organizes prediction discrepancies into a structured risk representation, preserving complementary evidence across temporal scales in token, local-statistic, and observation spaces. A task-adaptive detector uses anomaly labels to select and combine this evidence for the target task. Across anomaly detection benchmarks, HieraNTP improves VUS-PR by 12.0% on TSB-AD-U and 15.5% on TSB-AD-M relative to the strongest baselines, and achieves the highest composite score on both TAB tracks, with controlled comparisons supporting the value of retaining distinct evidence. Our code is available at https://github.com/blisky-li/HieraNTP.

Machine Learning.title: ISBC: Interpretable Sparse Binary Coding of Pretrained Text Embeddings
Machine Learning.summary:
arXiv:2611.00999v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Pretrained text embeddings encode semantic structure in high-dimensional continuous spaces whose coordinates are difficult to interpret. We introduce Interpretable Sparse Binary Coding (ISBC), which learns a small set of binary dimensions from frozen embeddings without taxonomy labels or downstream outcomes. A trainable encoder and affine decoder combine reconstruction with controls on activity, factor utilization, dependence, and activation uncertainty. Individual bits and their conjunctions select overlapping document groups; complete activation profiles provide finer contexts for conditional comparisons. We evaluate these representations across corpora, backbones, and code configurations through reconstruction, geometry, predictive probes, and document inspection. Empirical cases identify both distinctions within existing categories and shared content across their boundaries. In a mixed-domain corpus, the most frequent profiles predominantly identify source collections, while selected within-source comparisons reveal sentiment and migration contrasts. Selected associations persist in additional documents encoded without refitting. In an engagement application, bits alone improve prediction of log-transformed outcomes over a constant reference, while their combinations identify within-event content contrasts associated with engagement. The results support using binary coordinates and their combinations for empirical interpretation, with complete profiles providing a fine, partly initialization-dependent description rather than a unique discrete taxonomy.

Machine Learning.title: Jet-QSparse: Accelerating Agentic LLM Inference with 4-Bit Sparse Attention
Machine Learning.summary:
arXiv:2611.01022v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Long-horizon reasoning and agentic workloads strain KV-cache capacity and decode attention throughput. We present Jet-QSparse, a training-free method that combines compact NVFP4 cache storage with native FP4 query-key computation on Blackwell tensor cores. A dense scan scores the full key history and selects 128-token blocks for sparse FP16 value aggregation with FP32 accumulation, preserving higher precision in the output-forming step while enabling contiguous tile loads. Calibrated key centering and at most two BF16 pages per sequence and layer address quantization error; FP8 prefill uses a temporary arena while the persistent cache is packed directly from BF16 activations. Across four hybrid LLMs, a budget of 128 blocks per KV head shows no detected accuracy loss on the evaluated mathematical reasoning, coding, and agentic benchmarks, although some smaller budgets incur losses. With 64 blocks, Qwen3.8-27B achieves a $1.94\times$ end-to-end decode speedup over dense BF16 at 128K context and batch size 16 on one GB300, and the measured Qwen KV pools provide $2.58$-$2.76\times$ BF16's token capacity.

Machine Learning.title: Hierarchical Asynchronous Federated Learning over Space-Air-Ground Integrated Networks
Machine Learning.summary:
arXiv:2611.01025v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: With the emerging 6G paradigm where AI services operate over decentralized and resource-constrained edge infrastructure, performance of distributed learning algorithms remains a significant challenge. This paper proposes HAFL, a Low Earth Orbit (LEO) satellite-assisted hierarchical asynchronous Federated Learning (FL) framework, enabling resource-limited terrestrial clients to collaborate via Ground-Satellite Links (GSLs). Within this framework, LEO satellites serve multiple roles: as edge servers aggregating and broadcasting models, as clients accelerating training, and as high-throughput relays managing inter-satellite routing through Inter-Satellite Links (ISLs). Unlike conventional synchronous Jacobian-type updates, HAFL employs asynchronous Gauss-Seidel-type updates to enhance convergence speed. We provide theoretical convergences for convex, strongly convex, and nonconvex objectives, respectively, and formulate optimization problems to jointly determine optimal hyperparameters to minimize global training latency. Evaluations demonstrate that HAFL achieves faster initial convergence and comparable final performance for benchmark DNNs and datasets, offering promising FL systems across remote areas with 6G technologies, but much less global rounds and communication cost.

Machine Learning.title: ParaBlock++: Communication-Computation Parallel Blockwise Hierarchical Federated Learning
Machine Learning.summary:
arXiv:2611.01040v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: In the emerging 6G paradigm, where AI-driven services operate over decentralized and resource-constrained infrastructures, the convergence of distributed learning algorithms remains a significant challenge. This paper introduces $\mathrm{ParaBlock}$++, a low Earth orbit (LEO) satellite-assisted hierarchical federated learning (HFL) framework, enabling resource-limited terrestrial clients to collaboratively engage in federated learning (FL) via ground-satellite links (GSLs) supported by LEO satellite megaconstellations. Within this architecture, LEO satellites serve multiple roles: as edge servers aggregating and broadcasting models, as clients accelerating training, and as high-throughput relays managing inter-satellite routing through inter-satellite links (ISLs). Departing from conventional synchronous Jacobian-type updates, $\mathrm{ParaBlock}$++ employs asynchronous BCD-type updates to enhance convergence speed. We provide theoretical convergence guarantees for convex, strongly convex, and non-convex objectives, and formulate optimization problems to determine optimal cluster resource allocation and model partitioning for minimizing global training latency. Experimental evaluations demonstrate that $\mathrm{ParaBlock}$++ achieves faster initial convergence and comparable final performance for deep neural networks (DNNs) such as ResNet-18, offering promising directions for federated learning across geographically remote areas enabled by 6G technologies, but much less global rounds and communication cost.

Machine Learning.title: Entropy-Regularized Reinforcement Learning for the Regime-Switching Consumption-Investment Problem
Machine Learning.summary:
arXiv:2611.01046v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: This paper establishes an entropy-regularized reinforcement learning (ERRL) framework for the continuous-time consumption-investment problem under a regime-switching market model with general utility functions. By incorporating randomized exploratory policies and Shannon entropy regularization into the stochastic optimal control formulation, we derive closed-form representations for the optimal exploratory consumption and investment strategies. Specifically, the optimal investment strategy follows a multivariate Gaussian distribution, whereas the optimal consumption strategy takes the form of a Gibbs measure---which specializes to a Gamma distribution under logarithmic utility and a non-standard exponential distribution under power utility. Crucially, our theoretical analysis reveals that the classical deterministic optimal decisions correspond to the mode---rather than the mean---of these exploratory distributions. Furthermore, we establish the convergence of the exploratory value function to its classical unregularized counterpart as the temperature parameter vanishes. For algorithmic design, we develop a continuous-time q-learning framework grounded in a novel continuous-time q-function, prove the policy improvement theorem, and establish martingale characterizations for both on-policy and off-policy learning. We find that parameterizing the actor network based on theoretical distribution families can help accelerate convergence and enhance numerical stability. Furthermore, numerical experiments across regime-switching environments provide empirical support for our theoretical findings, demonstrating stable loss convergence as well as the monotonicity and concavity of the learned value functions.

Machine Learning.title: Infinite Worlds from One Example: What Local Generators Must Share
Machine Learning.summary:
arXiv:2611.01048v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Seeded noise lets games generate any region of an unbounded world on demand. We ask what such a generator needs when every small window must come from one example, the constraint behind Wave Function Collapse. The difficulty is that local constraints can require agreement over arbitrary distances: in a brick wall, each row keeps its place between the mortar lines. We study local generators, each cell a fixed function of the randomness near it. When the constraints carry a quantity that varies across the example, no generator that applies one rule, ignoring position, to independent randomness at every cell can be both exactly valid and faithful to the example's statistics, however far each cell reads. At radius r, staying faithful forces forbidden windows at a density of at least order 1/r, and a construction attains this order. To vary the quantity between exactly valid worlds, a generator needs randomness shared along its direction. We give a finitely checkable condition under which row types drawn from the seed and the position modulo a fixed period suffice for exact validity without learning. A search over the example's patches certifies these quantities and names the input each needs. Across 52 public examples of Wave Function Collapse and 27 from other implementations, it certifies only examples where a learned generator on independent randomness stays far from valid after repair. Given that input, a neural cellular automaton and a diffusion model become valid on 10 and 8 of the 12 certified examples that receive one, and on none from independent randomness. Valid means at most one forbidden window in a thousand after repair. With octaves of seeded noise elsewhere, the automaton is valid on 45 of the 52 public examples and 21 of the 27 from other implementations, and repair keeps random access.

Machine Learning.title: Efficient Conformal Calibration for Paired Recommendation Decisions
Machine Learning.summary:
arXiv:2611.01053v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Risk control can suppress useful changes to a frozen recommendation rule. We study how to recover valid activation from the same observed fractional losses. Two specified internal calibrators can lose efficiency by compressing losses into their sum or clipping auxiliary inverse counts before averaging. We propose Averaged Conformal Risk Calibration, or ACRC, which averages before clipping. A product identity proves expected-risk validity, while pointwise bounds characterize the additional activation. For fixed populations sampled without replacement, we connect activation to signed utility under heterogeneous users and switching constraints. Near the budgets, positive population mean gain and the stated nondegeneracy conditions give positive leading-order utility increments despite sampling dependence. Across six datasets, changing only calibration improves discounted net utility by $0.010226$ over raw and $0.008337$ over RB. A separately frozen Jester confirmation gives $0.011025 \pm 0.001082$ over raw with the rule and filter fixed, using a five-seed approximate 95 percent paired interval. Against information-matched SCoRE selecting risk or reward scores, the mean utility difference is $+0.015934 \pm 0.001440$. These gains use more mean realized risk within the declared budgets. Upstream failures delimit the benefit: efficient calibration releases useful modifications when the proposals themselves have value.

Machine Learning.title: On Sparse Graph Limits for Neural Combinatorial Optimization
Machine Learning.summary:
arXiv:2611.01069v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Graph neural networks are often trained on small graphs and deployed on larger ones, raising the question of which graph information must be preserved for combinatorial optimization values to transfer across sizes. We establish size-transfer guarantees for normalized graph optimization values using finite collections of energy features. For affine objectives, including MAX-CUT, coloring defect, and independent-set density, differences in task value are controlled by discrepancies in normalized scalar energy probes on all bounded-degree graphs. For general Lipschitz objectives, such as those with balance penalties, an additional representation error appears; this error vanishes on hyperfinite graph families but can remain bounded away from zero on expanders. Thus, at fixed degree bound, state space, Lipschitz constant, and target accuracy, a finite energy representation independent of graph size suffices universally for affine tasks and asymptotically for general Lipschitz tasks on hyperfinite families. These results yield prediction guarantees under explicit conditions on encoder accuracy, readout stability, and representation coverage, together with statistical generalization bounds. Theoretically, we prove Shapley-Folkman bounds with sharp parameter dependence, including a dimension-free $\ell_2$ regime, and realize the resulting energy features with a fixed-weight message-passing network using random node initialization on bounded-treewidth graphs. Experiments with exact solvers and trained models test the resulting transfer guarantees.

Machine Learning.title: Synergetic Autonomous Intelligence: Three Axioms for Recursive Semi-Closed Learning
Machine Learning.summary:
arXiv:2611.01070v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: We introduce Synergetic Autonomous Intelligence (SAI), a theory and design program for learning systems that form, preserve, revise, and compose relations while continuing to learn. SAI is built on three axioms: consequential distinctions must not become orphaned (U); identity is determined by future-faithful continuation under a declared contract (I); and unresolved defects are repaired by the least lawful local completion at the lowest admitted grade (L). We model a model, agent, tool, team, or environment boundary as a recursive semi-closed system with a Kernel-Ring representation, a Compile-Open-Participate cycle, and a typed residual comparing actual with claimed continuation. Under explicit finite or affine contracts, we establish relative consistency and conditional non-redundancy of U/I/L, characterize a contract-relative semantic quotient, construct an exact joint stochastic refinement, derive a constrained residual contraction, prove finite-horizon continued-service viability, and give an executed-intervention identification result with an observational-confounding boundary. We define GRC-Close as the generative and repair schema for this contract. The framework also gives finite contracts for action-effect-feedback loop re-entry, partial failure, duplicate-effect idempotency, replay, concurrent delivery, causal uncertainty, and threshold-radix state representation. KREIT, the Kernel-Ring Equilibrium Information Theory layer, treats information as a typed, resource-bounded distinction; the control layer authorizes, executes, audits, and updates actions across cloud-edge-end scales. These results establish a common contract-level vocabulary for representation, relation, memory, action, communication, explanation, coordination, and growth, while marking the assumptions and open boundaries required for later generalization.

Machine Learning.title: Change the Funnel, Not Who May Submit: Engineering Peer Review for the Flood
Machine Learning.summary:
arXiv:2611.01076v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Every reviewer knows the feeling: more papers each cycle, three full reviews for each of them, and a suspicion that near the accept line the outcome is luck. The numbers bear it out. NeurIPS received 30,709 submissions in 2026, more than three times as many as in 2021, and reviewing them took some 184,000 expert hours, or 92 years of researchers' time. Three-quarters of those hours went to papers that were rejected. And when NeurIPS twice had the same papers reviewed by two committees, the second rejected half of what the first accepted.
  Conferences are responding by limiting who may submit. We simulated that answer, and an alternative, in a model calibrated to the NeurIPS experiments. The limits save little and select no better, and those based on a past acceptance fall mostly on new authors. The alternative changes how papers are judged, spending full reads only where a decision turns on them. In a staged funnel, an automated quality check first turns back papers that are not ready. The rest are ranked by their value, from short summaries, by readers that each submission brings. Only the finalists get a full read, which checks their claims and settles the final ranking. The staged funnel needs a little over half of today's expert hours, accepts 95.5% of papers in the top 3-10% (against 74% today), and makes nearly every top-0.5% paper a spotlight or oral. And because every paper brings its own reader, the funnel keeps pace with the flood.

Machine Learning.title: Multi-Turn Semantic Caching for Low-Cost LLM Serving
Machine Learning.summary:
arXiv:2611.01077v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Semantic caching lowers the cost of serving large language models (LLMs) by reusing stored responses for similar requests. In multi-turn conversations, whether a cached response is acceptable depends on both conversations' histories, which embedding similarity of requests and histories predicts poorly (AUC 0.62--0.74 on five workloads). We therefore learn the \emph{reuse risk}, the probability that a cached response is unacceptable, from judge feedback, and choose a budgeted set of conversation states to cache by weighing the generation cost a reuse avoids against a price for unacceptable reuse. We propose CUCB-SC-MT, which learns a cache from logged conversations with a suboptimality guarantee, and CLCB-LS-MT, which learns online and has $\tilde O(\sqrt N)$ regret over $N$ requests when conversation states recur. On math-tutoring (SocraTeach) and movie-ticketing (Taskmaster-3) conversations, both achieve lower loss than prior semantic caching approaches: ContextCache, multi-turn variants of ElastiCache and vCache, and single-turn semantic caching at every cache budget. With 1,000 cache entries, CLCB-LS-MT avoids 35--41\% of the generation cost through acceptable reuses, against at most 22--25\% for the baselines, and lowers estimated serving latency by 19--35\%.

Machine Learning.title: Scute: Exact Batched Serving for PEFT Adapters Beyond LoRA
Machine Learning.summary:
arXiv:2611.01089v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Existing serving systems for large language models batch requests for many different LoRA adapters on one GPU. However, these systems reject adapters from other parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) methods such as DoRA, (IA), VeRA and OFT. One solution to this is to convert these adapters to LoRA, but this induces a significant memory and accuracy cost. Instead, we show that, under some modifications, a batched LoRA kernel can serve all of these methods exactly and efficiently. We achieve this by writing each method in one normal form, a LoRA computation with six slots for an adapter's own vectors and matrices. Some slots can merge into an adapter's weights at load time; the others remain live and induce a cost. We give ways to efficiently pay this cost and predict it from a zero-parameter byte model. We package this system, Scute, and build it on top of vLLM. Scute serves all five methods, coming as checkpoints from the Hugging Face PEFT library, in one batch, and it matches that library with a mean error of at most 1.5% of each adapter's effect. Under a burst of requests on an RTX A6000, a mix of these methods takes 5-17% more decode time than the same number of LoRA adapters. Furthermore, using Scute, the same GPU can serve 64 to 1024 (IA) and VeRA adapters at 1.5x to at least 2.5x the request rate of their LoRA conversions.

Machine Learning.title: Mitigating Catastrophic Forgetting in Task-Free Federated Continual Forecasting via Two-Tier Replay under Concept Drift
Machine Learning.summary:
arXiv:2611.01098v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Federated time-series forecasting is increasingly important in applications where temporal data are distributed across privacy-sensitive clients, such as environmental monitoring, smart cities, and industrial sensing. A central limitation of current continual-learning protocols is that they usually assume predefined task boundaries, whereas deployed forecasting systems receive an uninterrupted stream and must decide autonomously when adaptation is necessary. This paper addresses catastrophic forgetting in task-free federated forecasting under concept drift. We introduce a drift-aware continual-learning protocol in which each client monitors prediction-window RMSE, calibrates a robust median threshold from the offline base period, and triggers adaptation only after persistent degradation. To mitigate forgetting, we propose a TwoTierReplay mechanism that separates fixed offline representative memory from online memory. The offline tier preserves long-term knowledge learned during the base phase, while the online tier captures recent distributional changes after drift. Experiments on the Beijing Multi-Site Air- Quality dataset with 12 clients, three forecasting targets, and three horizons show that TwoTierReplay achieves the best stability-plasticity score in all nine target-horizon configurations. It improves over the strongest baseline by approximately 11.4%. These results suggest that explicit temporal structuring of replay memory is a practical and effective mechanism for task-free federated continual forecasting.

Machine Learning.title: Zero-Gated Cross-Attention
Machine Learning.summary:
arXiv:2611.01116v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Injecting non-text modalities into frozen language models often introduces early optimization instability, making it difficult to separate architectural gains from transient training dynamics. We introduce Inductively Gated Cross-Attention (IGCA), a zero-initialized cross-attention bridge that preserves pretrained model behavior at initialization while enabling gradual multimodal conditioning. Integrated across six decoder layers of frozen Falcon-40B, open_llama_30b, and Bloom-7b1 backbones (with 40,404,961,288 trainable adapter parameters used during training), IGCA acts as an exact algebraic no-op at initialization with a maximum output discrepancy of 0.00e+00. Over 59,500 training steps on Falcon-40B, the training loss decreases from 3.9403 to 0.0007 (with final ten step losses of [0.0001, 0.0003, 0.0005, 0.0002, 0.0005, 0.0011, 0.0005, 0.0006, 0.0005, 0.0007]). On held-out evaluation, the best gate-on checkpoint achieves a loss of 2.2201 compared to 4.3469 for the gate-off baseline -- a 48.9% reduction (2.1268 nats) -- while average held-out loss improves from 4.3423 to 2.2498 (1.9075 nats) with a mean gate magnitude of $\vert{}\tanh(\alpha)\vert{} = 0.0713$.

Machine Learning.title: World Models Need Not Be Right to Rank Policies Right: Relative Bounds and Audit Limits
Machine Learning.summary:
arXiv:2611.01139v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Selecting a reinforcement-learning (RL) policy usually requires additional environment interaction, while learned world models offer cheap but potentially biased evaluations. This raises two distinct questions: can shared model errors preserve pairwise rankings despite poor absolute values, and do they make a small number of real audits more informative? We derive an exact pairwise simulation identity and a relative bound separating common-mode Bellman residuals from policy-specific error. The analysis motivates RAVEL (Relative Auditing of Value Errors in Learned models), a selective policy tournament whose eliminations use held-out real outcomes. We test 45 SAC, TD3, and PPO policies per task in DMC cheetah-run and walker-walk. At rollout horizon 500, model rankings remain strong (Kendall tau = 0.962 and 0.800), and same-run differential-error ratios are 0.674 and 0.106. Yet mean paired audit-error correlations are only 0.007 and 0.090, and pairing changes standard deviation by -2.5 percent and +1.9 percent. Simultaneous intervals attain 99.98 percent and 99.75 percent coverage, but certify only 13.2 percent and 0 percent of decisions at eight audits. RAVEL improves low-budget walker-walk regret, whereas real-only successive halving is better at the largest budget, rejecting the precommitted twofold efficiency target. Frozen-model optimization lowers real return without increasing predicted return on average. Thus ranking fidelity, useful audit covariance, and upward model exploitation are distinct properties, separated in part by closed-loop trajectory divergence.
Machine Learning.comment: Comments: 10 pages, 2 figures, 2 tables. Accepted as a poster at the NeurIPS 2026 Workshop on World Models in Physical AI

Machine Learning.title: Lightweight Representation Learning for Low Tucker Rank Tensors
Machine Learning.summary:
arXiv:2611.01168v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Low Tucker rank tensors provide compact representations of multidimensional dependencies, but standard learning pipelines can incur substantial computational and memory overhead from redundant intermediate quantities. We reduce this overhead without modifying the underlying representation objective or parameterization. Our approach combines three complementary components: (i) sequential extraction of only task-required spectral components, avoiding unnecessary full decompositions; (ii) factor-wise multilinear contractions without materializing large Kronecker operators; and (iii) compact latent-state updates without storing full ambient tensor iterates. These components preserve the algebraic operations and learning trajectories of the original algorithms while reducing their computational and memory footprints. Across five low Tucker rank tensor estimators, our implementations match the original trajectories to numerical precision (relative discrepancies of $10^{-16}$ to $10^{-13}$), while reducing per-iteration runtime by up to $3.12\times$ and resident memory by up to $616\times$ ($99.8\%$) on the main order-3 benchmark at $n=100$, with memory reductions exceeding $900\times$ across the full evaluation suite. These results show that substantial computational redundancy can be eliminated from Tucker representation learning without changing the underlying model or learned representation.

Machine Learning.title: TRIAGE: Reliability- and Load-Conditioned Escalation for Two-Tier LLM Serving with a Semantic Evidence Judge
Machine Learning.summary:
arXiv:2611.01174v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Two-tier LLM serving escalates selected requests from a small model to a large one, but prompt-based routers cannot see whether retrieved evidence supports an answer, and they treat the GPU cost of an escalation as constant. We study TRIAGE, which conditions escalation on a post-generation reliability state and on a load-dependent GPU price, and we report both what held and what did not on one A40 serving Qwen2.5-7B and 32B (AWQ) under VLLM. Escalation cost rose 21.9x from 1 to 10 requests/s but showed no monotone dependence on KV-cache headroom, and a pre-registered claim that the reliability state detects corrupted evidence (AUROC>=0.70) was falsified at 0.571, although any prompt-only router scores exactly 0.500 by construction. Post hoc, a semantic evidence judge raised detection to 0.846 (0.926 on never-served items) and predicted wrong small-model answers at AUROC 0.90-0.96 on RGB and three RouterBench model pairs; the resulting cascade stayed within about 3 pp of GPT-4 at 79.5% lower API cost for GPT-3.5->GPT-4, yet fell below random routing for open-model pairs with 2-3x price ratios. End to end, the 7B->32B pair showed only a +2.88 pp held-out gap, so the allocator rightly declined to escalate and the headline is a null that a small pre-launch gate failed to expose.

Machine Learning.title: Fast and Exact Relative-Position Attention via Structure-Aware Kernels
Machine Learning.summary:
arXiv:2611.01182v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Relative-position attention mechanisms offer compelling alternatives to RoPE across various transformer architectures, delivering superior performance in domains such as audio. These mechanisms typically modify attention scores by adding content-position or bias-position terms. Unlike RoPE, which encodes position via per-token rotations directly on the queries and keys, relative-position terms generally require pairwise offset-dependent computation or lookups, complicating their integration into fused attention kernels and introducing severe memory, bandwidth, and compute overheads as sequences scale. To address this bottleneck, we propose an exact attention algorithm that incorporates additive relative-position terms into FlashAttention-style tiled computation. Our method (1) uses offset-aware tiling to avoid redundant indexing and memory accesses, (2) computes only the necessary key/query-relation products and reuses them across token pairs in both forward and backward passes, and (3) uses offset-based gradient sharding and aggregation, eliminating atomic contention. We provide a unified, efficient Triton implementation across diverse relative-position attention mechanisms and evaluate it against naive and specialized implementations. For 8K-token sequences, our method speeds up the forward (backward) pass by 1.8-6.4$\times$ (2.0-21$\times$) and reduces peak memory up to 2.9-128$\times$ (1.4-54$\times$) over the strongest baseline for each mechanism, enabling long-context end-to-end transcription that is 1.8$\times$ faster and uses 2.4$\times$ less memory. Our method thus provides a drop-in, hardware-efficient solution for scaling relative-position attention transformers.

Machine Learning.title: Satisfied, Not Solving: Wireheading of Bounded Homeostatic Rewards in Reinforcement Learning
Machine Learning.summary:
arXiv:2611.01183v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Bounded intrinsic rewards are often assumed to be safe from exploitation: if a signal can yield at most a fixed amount, gaming it should not pay. We test this for a homeostatic satiation reward, in which needs build up and relieving them is rewarding, and give the agent a cheap action that resets its needs. In MiniGrid DoorKey-8x8, PPO agents with this action solved 2 of 80 seeds, against 71 of 80 on the same seeds without it; in KeyCorridorS3R1, 0 of 20 against 20 of 20. Their policies stayed near uniform. The reward does not ask for this: a telescoping argument caps any policy's satiation return at the needs' starting drive, and a post-hoc computation shows that, at every growth rate we trained, a solving trajectory beats that cap on all sampled layouts. In DoorKey with advantage normalization on, a satisfaction signal the agent could fill itself was worse than none (11 of 20 solved with task reward alone, 1 of 20 with the tamperable signal), and a per-press cost of 0.1 restored the task in every seed. Farming of positive reward cycles appeared in DoorKey but not persistently in KeyCorridorS3R1. All predictions were pre-registered, and hash-locked from round 3 on; 9 of our 23 hypotheses were not supported, and we report each.

Machine Learning.title: Zeroth-Order Policy Optimization for Scheduling in Queueing Networks
Machine Learning.summary:
arXiv:2611.01186v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Reinforcement learning in queueing network scheduling presents significant challenges because of the countably infinite state space and the high stochasticity in transitions. In this paper, we propose zeroth-order policy optimization algorithms that are easy to implement and rely solely on estimates of the average cost, a single scalar quantity, without requiring the estimation of value or advantage functions. Our analysis focuses on back-pressure guarded policies and establishes uniform smoothness of the average cost objective with respect to the policy parameters. Building on this property, we establish finite-time convergence guarantees to an $\epsilon$-stationary policy for the proposed algorithms. Numerical experiments on multiple queueing networks, including systems beyond classical exponential service distribution, demonstrate competitive performance, outperforming gradient-based RL methods like PPO and traditional queueing baselines.

Machine Learning.title: GraCo: A Unified Toolkit of Graph Coarsening Algorithms and Metrics
Machine Learning.summary:
arXiv:2611.01200v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Graph coarsening aims to reduce a graph to a smaller one that preserves chosen properties of the original. It is increasingly used to scale graph learning to large graphs, as a non-differentiable step applied once before training. Many coarsening methods have been proposed in recent years, each with its own implementation, notation and evaluation. In this work, we introduce GraCo, a unified toolkit of graph coarsening methods. It relies on a single definition: a coarsening is fixed by a partition of the nodes and by the Laplacian the coarsened graph is consistent with. The coarsened graph, and the reduction and lifting matrices that map signals from the original graph to the coarsened one and back, follow from these two choices. We implement 17 methods from the literature and a random baseline, grouped into five families, with the same notation, inputs and outputs. We also build a collection of metrics from different papers, applicable to any coarsening. We check the implementations on a synthetic stochastic block model, then we report the runtime and peak memory of each method on Cora, PubMed, ogbn-arxiv and ogbn-products. GraCo is open-source and available at https://github.com/Antonin-J/graco.

Machine Learning.title: A Batched Hartigan's $k$-Means Clustering
Machine Learning.summary:
arXiv:2611.01207v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Hartigan's $k$-means algorithm has theoretical advantages over the standard Lloyd's variant, which has become synonymous with "$k$-means". Yet, Hartigan's algorithm is far slower in practice due to its inherently sequential calculations. We devise a Batched Hartigan's method that enables vectorized calculation by exploiting the triangle inequality to expose a set of parallel-safe updates and a smaller set of sequential updates. This makes Hartigan's method competitive with Lloyd's in execution speed for the first time.
Machine Learning.comment: Comments: To appear in the 40th Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS 2026)

Machine Learning.title: Mathematical Formulation and Comparative Performance Evaluation of Machine Learning Algorithms for Maize Land Suitability Prediction
Machine Learning.summary:
arXiv:2611.01239v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Addressing the food needs of a growing population is one of the major challenges of developing countries like Ethiopia. Various policies aimed at increasing food production have been enacted by governments and development partners. Although efforts in this regard have been made, there is still inadequate emphasis on increasing food production through the use of high technology practices. Precision agriculture using technology has been utilized to increase crop yield. Precision agriculture also relies on identifying land for a crop, which is a key factor that affects crop yield. Traditional methods of assessing land suitability for crop production are time-consuming, costly and unreliable. Against this background, the aim of this study was to assess the potential of machine learning (ML) in improving the speed and accuracy of assessing land suitability for maize, a staple crop in Ethiopia, as compared to traditional methods. The study is investigated in three areas (Burie, Shindi and Tilili) in the Amhara region. Data collection was done through the local agriculture offices and survey teams. The data were coded, scaled and balanced. Various feature extraction techniques, which included Univariate Feature Selection(UFS), Recursive Feature Elimination with Cross-Validation(RFECV) and Sequential Feature Selection(SFS), and various classifiers, which were K-nearest neighbor (KNN), gradient boosting (GB),random forest (RF) with mathematical formulations were employed. The best models were constructed through combining GBOOST and SFS and achieved an accuracy of 99.41% and 99.35% for both precision and recall. Our results showed that using machine learning is a reliable method of assessing land suitability for maize in Ethiopia.
  Keywords: Maize, Gradient boosting,Land suitability,Machine learning, Mathematical formulations

Machine Learning.title: Learning What to Ask and What to Believe: Distilling a Variational Bayesian Agent into Language Models
Machine Learning.summary:
arXiv:2611.01245v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Interactive tasks such as eliciting a user's preferences or diagnosing a hidden mechanism require an agent to track its uncertainty over a latent state, ask informative questions and act on the answers. Language models have no explicit mechanism for this, whereas Bayesian information seeking provides one through posterior inference and expected information gain (EIG), and we ask whether it can be distilled into an 8B language model. Our teacher, a lightweight Bayesian agent with a sequential variational belief and EIG query selection, matches or approaches exact and particle references on three task families. We generate synthetic interactions with the teacher on episodes disjoint from the benchmark and fine-tune \Student{} to reproduce its queries and its belief state as a structured scratchpad. On three Multi-Turn Puzzles tasks the student raises Circuit Decoding from 0.00 to 0.93 success, lowers the normalized rank of the recommended film from 0.50 to 0.10 and cuts word guessing from 32 to 3.4 attempts, exceeding the strongest reported language models on the two comparable tasks. Exposing the belief state closes much of the gap where the decision is an implicit computation rather than a read-out of the interaction; in matched teacher contrasts, EIG supervision consistently outperforms random querying, whereas greater inference fidelity does not uniformly improve the distilled student; a 70B language-model teacher does not match the Bayesian teacher in downstream student performance, and the learned skill does not transfer to an unseen task family. Variational Bayesian information seeking can thus be amortized into a language model by transferring the belief state that drives its questions and decisions.

Machine Learning.title: LoRAForge: Co-Designing Post-Hoc Compression and Execution for Efficient Multi-LoRA Serving
Machine Learning.summary:
arXiv:2611.01256v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Multi-LoRA serving allows many task-specific adapters to share a common base model, but scaling to large adapter fleets introduces substantial storage, loading, and execution overheads. Post-hoc compression can reduce the memory footprint of trained LoRA adapters, yet smaller ranks do not automatically translate into faster serving. For instance, padding, factor access, and generic kernels can obscure the retained low-rank structure, while independently recompressing thousands of modules also incurs significant preparation overhead. We present LoRAForge, a system connecting batched factor construction to rank-specialized execution through an explicit retained-rank representation. It supports two allocation policies: uniform retention ratios (LoRAForge-U) and spectral-energy budget allocation (LoRAForge-S). Both share FlashTSQR factor construction and the same serving backend. FlashTSQR exploits parallelism across modules and row tiles, accelerating factor construction by up to $2.28\times$ over matched library QR. In a fixed-work Qwen control, the shared runtime adds $1.17$--$1.22\times$ throughput across both compressed policies, with negligible gains on original adapters. Across 85 trained open-weighted Qwen and Llama adapters, the spectral policy's floored quality configuration retains about 7.7% of adapter parameters with fleet-average score drops of at most 1.2 points on a 0--100 scale. The same rank-floored $1/12$ spectral exports achieve substantial token-throughput gains on both AMD and NVIDIA GPUs.

Machine Learning.title: Does Random Search Discover Task Experts? Revisiting Neural Thickets
Machine Learning.summary:
arXiv:2611.01262v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Pretrained models are typically viewed as generalists, requiring bespoke post-training to achieve task-specific expertise. Gan & Isola (2026) recently proposed a striking alternative: that pretrained models lie in a dense neural thicket of task specialists, which can be surfaced with simple Gaussian weight perturbations. We examine this neural thicket of task-specific experts and identify several key findings that question this perspective. First, we find that the apparent lift of the best-of-N selected perturbation decays quickly with selection-set size m, strongly suggesting overfitting to the selection questions. In fact, for 10 of the 12 model-task pairs we study, a simple null model of pure selection noise predicts more than 75 percent of the top expert's reward lift. Second, the top experts' advantage often vanishes on held-out questions or remains within the run-to-run variability of the unperturbed pretrained model. Third, we find that majority voting over the top-K selected perturbations, termed RandOpt(N, K) by Gan & Isola (2026), is often matched or outperformed by majority voting over K samples from the base model. Overall, our results suggest that random weight perturbations may be ineffective at uncovering task experts around pretrained models, and that task adaptation requires more sophistication than random search. Code and artifacts are available at github.com/asil012/RevisitingNeuralThickets.

Machine Learning.title: Learning momenta for Hamiltonian-based models
Machine Learning.summary:
arXiv:2611.01269v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: There has been increasing interest in methodologies that incorporate physics priors into neural network architectures to enhance their modeling capabilities. Among these methodologies, Hamiltonian neural networks (HNNs) and their variants have gained considerable attention. These architectures explicitly encode Hamiltonian mechanics both in their structure and loss function, resulting in desirable properties and additional modeled information. A crucial limitation of HNNs is their reliance on data on the target system's generalized momenta. This severely hampers their applicability when the analytical form of the generalized momenta is unknown, which frequently is the case in real-world applications. The goal of the present work is to develop a general extension of Hamiltonian-based architectures that addresses this issue by simultaneously learning the system's generalized momenta, Hamiltonian structure, and dynamics from data. The proposed architecture learns the generalized momenta when their analytical form is unknown, and only (potentially non-sequential) data on the state and its derivatives is available. A dissipative mass-spring system, a double pendulum, and a rolling disk under nonholonomic constraints are considered as canonical examples to assess the performance of the proposed architecture.

Machine Learning.title: Geometry of Confabulation and Refusal in Small Language Models
Machine Learning.summary:
arXiv:2611.01272v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Faced with an unanswerable question, small language models can either refuse or confabulate: confidently produce a wrong answer. Can the hidden state before the first generated token provide a clue? Can we flip confabulations into refusals? I introduce ConfabQA, a 784-item benchmark whose obscure-pre-cutoff category breaks the typical correctness/knowledge-cutoff confound and map the geometry of the hidden state with linear probes, a sparse autoencoder (SAE), and direct optimization of intervention directions. On Qwen3-1.7B and Gemma 2 2B the probe separates upcoming refusals from confabulations well beyond prompt features (+7.4/+16.3 pp); on Llama 3.2 3B the ConfabQA margin is within fold-to-fold spread, but a direct refusal probe on PopQA and TriviaQA recovers +18-25 pp. On Qwen I closely inspect three candidate directions for the refusal vector: probe-recovered, Qwen-Scope SAE feature, and directly optimized. Although the three directions are pairwise 50-81 degrees apart, a push at or below the state's own norm along any of them flips most confabulations into refusal openings dominated by the "As..." family. Forcing the opener without touching the hidden state yields the same one-in-three judged-refusal rate as any push. The opposite push collapses refusals mostly into confabulations, yet leaves originally correct answers intact, so the direction gates the opening speech act rather than the knowledge behind it. Confabulations do not resolve into a concentrated feature in a dictionary or a token signature on Qwen3-1.7B. Scoring every probe on the margin over the strongest of four prompt-feature baselines extracts the hidden state's own contribution. Correctness signal is model-dependent and portable only for Llama 3.2 3B: 81% of the probe's margin over test majority survives transfer between ConfabQA, PopQA, and TriviaQA. Benchmark, judge, and code are released.

Machine Learning.title: Best-of-Both-Worlds FTRL for Linear Bandits: The Interplay of Information Acquisition, Corruption, and Geometry
Machine Learning.summary:
arXiv:2611.01299v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: We study \textit{best-of-both-worlds} (BOBW) algorithms for linear bandits, which aim to simultaneously guarantee $\gO(\sqrt T)$ regret in the adversarial regime and $\gO(\log T)$ regret in the stochastic regime over $T$ rounds. For finite action sets, we introduce \emph{information-acquisition follow-the-regularized-leader} (\IAFTRL{}), the first BOBW algorithm based purely on the follow-the-regularized-leader (FTRL) framework that attains an $\gO(\cstar\log T)$-type regret in the stochastic regime, where $\cstar$ is the information-acquisition complexity that characterizes instance-dependent optimality in linear bandits, while retaining the $\gO(\sqrt{T})$ regret guarantee in the adversarial regime. This resolves the open problem posed in~\cite{LeeEtAl2021,KongZ023,ItoT23,ZhaoItoLi2025}.

Machine Learning.title: Accelerating posterior sampling in Bayesian inverse problems with diffusion models: an online-offline perspective
Machine Learning.summary:
arXiv:2611.01300v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Bayesian inverse problems require both informative prior models and computationally feasible posterior inference. Score-based diffusion models provide expressive learned priors, but their use for inversion introduces a conditioning problem: the score of a noised posterior is generally unavailable from a prior score alone. This selective survey reviews the principal approaches to that problem, including likelihood guidance, spectral and projection methods, sequential Monte Carlo corrections, and amortized conditional training. We organize methods by how they split cost between offline preparation and online inference, and compare their assumptions, advantages and limitations, with emphasis on computational speedups. Some ongoing directions and open questions are gathered at the end.

Machine Learning.title: When Does Exploration Prevent Collapse? Three Regimes and the Path of the Reward in Self-Consistency Training
Machine Learning.summary:
arXiv:2611.01307v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Test-time reinforcement learning (TTRL) adapts a model without labels by rewarding answers that agree with the majority, but it collapses the policy onto its majority answer and can remove the correct answer from the samples. Exploration can prevent this collapse, yet its strength is chosen by trial and error, and how the training algorithm changes the required strength is unclear. We model training on a single problem as a continuous flow of the logits of a softmax policy and analyze which policies are stable as the exploration coefficient varies. Only collapsed policies are stable below a lower boundary and only policies spread over many answers above an upper boundary, and we derive these boundaries in closed form for an agreement reward with smoothing toward the uniform policy, compute them for the majority reward of TTRL on policies with one leading answer and bound them with interval arithmetic for actions on ordered bins. We prove that under exact gradients, the learning rate and, in a mean-field model, the normalization of GRPO leave these boundaries unchanged when exploration passes through them together with the reward but shift them when exploration bypasses them. Exact sums on these policies then show that a bonus for rare answers needs a coefficient above $1/\log(G-1)$ for groups of $G$ samples before the normalization and about two to three times that after it. In free-form TTRL on MATH-500, a bonus placed before the normalization prevented collapse and kept more correct answers among the samples, although it lowered pass@1.

Machine Learning.title: AgentCBO: Causal Belief Routing for Bayesian Optimization under Unknown Graphs
Machine Learning.summary:
arXiv:2611.01317v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Causal Bayesian optimization (CBO) typically relies on the unrealistic assumption of a perfectly known causal graph. Recent methods relax this constraint by coupling optimization with structure learning, but they often waste sample budgets on structural uncertainties that are irrelevant to the optimizer. In this paper, we formalize routing-equivalence to shift the objective from full causal-graph recovery to causal belief routing, where structural differences only matter when they alter optimizer-facing objects such as admissible exploration sets and do-priors. Furthermore, we propose agentcbo, a graph-belief routing framework that incorporates LLM causal priors through guarded proposal and commit mechanisms. Specifically, a Language-Prior Agent combines LLM beliefs with constraint-based discovery to extract a protected causal backbone alongside residual uncertain edges. A Calibration Agent and a Residual Repair Agent then refine only these uncertain structures through score-gated bounded local edits. Finally, a deterministic commit gate evaluates candidate updates using routing-proxy checks before allowing them to influence intervention selection. Across ten benchmarks, agentcbo performs comparably to known-graph CBO, demonstrating that guarded LLM priors can improve fixed-budget CBO performance.

Machine Learning.title: Inferring missing locations in human mobility data using memory effects
Machine Learning.summary:
arXiv:2611.01319v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Empirical datasets used to characterize human mobility are sparse in space and time, owing to technological factors such as coverage and battery, or to the erratic nature of online interactions. Missing data can bias the conclusions drawn from them, so filling the gaps in incomplete timelines is a key challenge in computational social science. Here, we propose a simple imputation method in which the informativeness of an observation decays with its bidirectional temporal distance from the missing entry, at a rate set by a single parameter per individual. On synthetic and real Twitter data, a power-law decay, selected by Bayesian model comparison, yields accurate imputations (macro-AUROC above 0.9 overall, and above 0.8 for the most mobile users) and matches a gap-aware continuous-time Markov chain, outperforming it among the most mobile users. The method is robust to moderate noise and generalizes across countries and European administrative regions.

Machine Learning.title: Alignment Flywheel-Guided Suppression Patching for Interactionless Inverse Reinforcement Learning
Machine Learning.summary:
arXiv:2611.01322v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Learned reward models allow reinforcement-learning agents to use demonstrations, implicit feedback, safety constraints, social norms, or other sources that do not provide a complete hand-designed scalar reward.
