Machine Learning.title: A Deep Reinforcement Learning Framework for Real-Time Electric Vehicle Charging Management in IoEV-Enabled Smart Cities
Machine Learning.summary:
arXiv:2611.01751v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: The rapid growth of electric vehicles (EVs) in urban environments demands intelligent, decentralised charging management strategies that operate under strict real-time constraints. This paper proposes an Edge-Intelligent architecture in which each EV selects a charging station (CS) by querying a shared, centrally trained Deep Q-Network (DQN) policy over a lightweight MQTT publish-subscribe backbone; independent per-EV edge inference is the deployment target, not the configuration evaluated here. The reported simulation evaluates that shared DQN policy applied sequentially to each vehicle's observations within a single SUMO run, using MQTT for KPI telemetry while observations are obtained through TraCI. The system is evaluated on two real-world road networks from OpenStreetMap (Rabat Agdal-Hay Riad and Tangier, Morocco); the primary network carries four geolocated public charging stations with heterogeneous power levels (50 kW and 150 kW). Three traffic demand profiles (morning, midday, evening peak) are simulated, and four decision policies are compared: an Adaptive Heuristic, a Tabular Q-Learning agent, the proposed DQN agent, and a Double DQN variant. A multi-seed statistical protocol (7 seeds, Wilcoxon signed-rank test, Cohen's d) evaluates the results. The DQN agent achieves a 6.8% relative improvement in charge rate and a 5.4% increase in delivered energy over the Adaptive Heuristic under Evening Peak demand ($p = 0.016$, Cohen's $d = 0.99$ and $1.51$), while showing no advantage in waiting time; on the second network the heuristic leads on waiting time, so the ranking is not stable across geographies. A scalability analysis shows linear state-space growth with station count and sub-millisecond inference; all runs include intermittent station outages under a Markov failure process.

Machine Learning.title: ReCoG: Relative Node Contexts for Multi-Domain Graph Pre-training
Machine Learning.summary:
arXiv:2611.01753v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: The success of foundation models in language and vision has motivated Graph Foundation Models (GFMs), which learn transferable knowledge through multi-domain graph pre-training. Existing methods advance GFMs through feature unification and structural learning, and in doing so they rely on the raw graph structure to organize node contexts. However, we observe that removing a large proportion of edges from source graphs during pre-training improves cross-domain transfer accuracy across four representative methods. Our theoretical analysis identifies the raw graph structure as a source of conflict in cross-graph model sharing. We therefore advocate defining node contexts using criteria consistent across graphs. Achieving this requires (1) constructing node contexts consistently across graphs without a shared positional structure, such as the token order of text or the pixel grid of images, and (2) retaining the structural and neighborhood information of the original graphs. To this end, we introduce Relative Contexts for Graphs (ReCoG) for multi-domain graph pre-training. Specifically, we first construct attribute contexts to provide a comparison rule independent of the raw graph structure. Furthermore, we construct structural contexts based on common neighbors and semantic contexts based on neighborhood attribute summaries to retain the topological and neighborhood information of the original graphs. Since all graphs share these construction rules, we pre-train a single graph encoder by reconstructing node attributes over these contexts, without domain-specific modules. We conduct extensive experiments on 18 target datasets, which demonstrate the effectiveness of ReCoG. In particular, ReCoG exceeds the strongest baseline by 7.61 percentage points in mean 1-shot cross-domain node classification accuracy and by 4.47 points in cross-type transfer to heterophilous graphs.

Machine Learning.title: Silent Reward and Environment Defects in EV Charging Simulation Benchmarks: A Diagnostic Checklist
Machine Learning.summary:
arXiv:2611.01769v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Reinforcement-learning (RL) benchmarks built on microscopic traffic simulators such as SUMO are increasingly used to compare agent architectures for electric vehicle (EV) charging assignment. Unlike crashes, defects in the reward function, the environment's stochastic model, or the state encoding often fail silently: the simulation completes, produces plausible numbers, and the comparison is biased. We report five such defects, found by auditing a five-agent benchmark on OpenStreetMap road networks, stated generically: a shared random generator that desynchronises seed-paired comparisons, an ablation-specific reward clip applied unconditionally, a normalisation mismatch that zeroes a reward term, a per-timestep penalty that should fire once per event, and a state dimensionality documented but never wired into the network. We quantify three: a rejection counter inflated up to 125x across agents/cities, a reward term bounded at about $10^{-4}$ of its intended scale, and a 16.6%/16.3% greedy-action divergence from a state-encoding mismatch. Re-analysing a historical ablation, no A1-A2 effect survives family-wise correction; a 56-run campaign confirms the RNG defect's mechanism directly while showing its correction does not change that conclusion. We provide an eight-item checklist as a low-cost first-pass audit; in a later regeneration, three checks caught two new defects while three further process/artefact defects fell outside its boundary.

Machine Learning.title: Spectral Signatures of Memorization Basins in Diffusion Trajectories
Machine Learning.summary:
arXiv:2611.01775v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Diffusion models are known to reproduce individual examples from their training data as a form of memorization with implications for generalization, privacy, and downstream use. Recent work demonstrated that memorized training samples reside inside contiguous regions of the data/latent space known as basins of memorization -- once a denoising trajectory enters a basin, under finite perturbations it irreversibly reproduces a memorized example. Prior empirical work on such basins in trained models has primarily focused on classifier-free guidance based detection and mitigation strategies in text-to-image models, leaving basin entry and their formation largely uncharacterized. In this paper, we present a geometric characterization of memorization basins for conditional, unconditional, and rectified-flow-based diffusion models. We observe a characteristic signature in the local spectrum of the function geometry that distinguishes basin entry: the emergence of a dominant singular mode followed by a sharp spectral recovery. This signature appears at two timescales: along denoising trajectories during inference and over the course of training. We further investigate whether these geometric signatures can be used to intervene on memorization. During training, we suppress memorization by acting on the dominant mode. At inference, we develop methods to identify trajectories entering memorization basins and steer them away. We find that these interventions remain effective even with low-dimensional approximations of the underlying geometry, and demonstrate that geometry-informed steering extends to large-scale text-to-image diffusion models. Together, our results corroborate that local spectral geometry provides a common basis for characterizing memorization and for suppressing, detecting, and steering away from it across training and generation.

Machine Learning.title: ReFrame: Silence-Aware Compute Reclamation for Full-Duplex Speech Models
Machine Learning.summary:
arXiv:2611.01835v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Full-duplex speech models execute dense model inference for every audio frame throughout a live interaction. This uniform framewise schedule creates sustained GPU load across dialogue states whose computation has strong, reusable temporal structure. ReFrame formulates full-duplex inference as a silence-aware computation problem. Mutual Silence Speculation (MSS) operates when both participants are silent: it evaluates multi-frame Temporal continuations, verifies text and hidden-state stability, and applies batched Mimi audio-token correction. Listening Frame Folding (LFF) operates while the user speaks and the agent listens: it processes already-arrived user frames through parallel Temporal execution and frame-batched audio-token generation while accepting only the verified prefix. Frame-Budget Reinvestment (FBR) assigns the released frame intervals to resumable external retrieval and language-model workers, then injects timely references through Moshi's conditioning interface. We instantiate ReFrame on five full-duplex models spanning Moshi-family, phase-structured, and flattened autoregressive generation. Across the complete 1,225-conversation FDBench, ReFrame reduces measured GPU execution time by 18.80-31.01% and retains 96.92-100% non-PAD text agreement on five different models. On HaluEval tests, FBR increases the number of correct generated spoken answers from 86 to 205 under the same auxiliary-service budget. ReFrame turns recurring dialogue structure into lower inference cost and higher end-to-end service capability.

Machine Learning.title: Missingness-Aware Prior-Data Fitted Network for Irregular Clinical Time-Series
Machine Learning.summary:
arXiv:2611.01851v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Clinical time series are irregularly observed with laboratory measurements recorded at uneven intervals and observation patterns often reflecting patient state, clinical concern, and site-specific practice. Consequently, missingness is not merely a nuisance factor but an informative signal for prediction. We propose a Missingness-Aware Prior-Data Fitted Network (MA-PFN) for irregular clinical time-series prediction. MA-PFN first learns a diffusion-based prior over joint laboratory value and observation-mask trajectories from source-domain electronic health records, capturing both physiological dynamics and measurement processes. Synthetic trajectories sampled from this prior are then transformed into context-query tasks to train a PFN-style conditional predictor. Once trained, the model performs prediction for new admissions in a single forward pass, requiring neither retraining nor parameter adaptation on target datasets. The framework naturally supports both imputation and forecasting through different context-query constructions. We conduct internal validation on a held-out MIMIC-III test set and external validation on eICU, evaluating both imputation and forecasting and assessing cross-domain generalization under shifts in patient populations, clinical practices, and observation mechanisms. MA-PFN achieves the best performance across all evaluated settings, with Overall/Macro nRMSD ranging from (0.193/0.186) for internal imputation to (0.297/0.297) for external forecasting, without target-domain adaptation. These results demonstrate that learning missingness-aware task priors enables accurate and transferable clinical time-series prediction under informative missingness.

Machine Learning.title: Privacy-Preserving ECG-HRV Emotion Classification for Mood Swing Detection using Federated Learning on Constrained Edge Devices
Machine Learning.summary:
arXiv:2611.01853v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: This paper presents a privacy-preserving mood monitoring framework that classifies emotional states from ECG-derived heart rate variability (HRV) features. The framework is evaluated on three public datasets comprising 74 participants and further validated using a wearable device in a pilot study. Leave-One-Participant-Out cross-validation (LOPO-CV) is used to assess generalization to unseen individuals. A series of experiments investigates the impact of temporal windowing, HRV feature selection, and class balancing on both four-class valence-arousal and binary valence classification. Results show that class balancing substantially improves minority-class recall, while Logistic Regression consistently outperforms five alternative classifiers and achieves competitive performance against HRV-based baselines. Pilot validation using a Polar H10 wearable achieves 75% binary valence accuracy on an unseen individual without calibration, demonstrating the feasibility of real-world deployment. To preserve privacy, the framework is also implemented using federated learning on a six-node Raspberry Pi cluster. Federated Logistic Regression achieves performance comparable to centralized training without sharing raw physiological data. These results demonstrate the potential of interpretable and privacy-preserving mood monitoring for continuous mental health assessment in clinical and community settings.

Machine Learning.title: Quantizing Recurrent Language Models Is Easier Than You Think
Machine Learning.summary:
arXiv:2611.01864v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Linear recurrences are becoming an increasingly common building block in large language models, replacing the growing KV cache of softmax attention with a fixed-size recurrent state that enables efficient decoding. However, the quantization stack has largely been developed around softmax Transformers, whose numerical properties and inference state differ from those of recurrent models. Our goal is to understand these differences and study the design space of quantization methods for recurrent models. In our analysis, we differentiate between two targets. First, extra-state quantization concerns weights and activations outside the recurrent state, whose distributions are shaped indirectly by the sequence mixer during training. In controlled 1.3B parameter models, we find that decayed recurrences develop weaker residual outlier channels than softmax attention and are therefore easier to quantize without incoherence processing. Second, intra-state quantization concerns the recurrent state itself during decode, where repeated updates create a different numerical problem from KV cache quantization. We instantiate our findings as LoReS, a state quantization pipeline combining value-axis scale grouping to match output channel magnitude, decay-based mixed-precision to protect slowly decaying heads or channels, and stochastic rounding to limit error accumulation under repeated requantization. Across Qwen-3.5 9B, Nemotron-H 8B, and Kimi-Linear 48B-A3B, LoReS supports robust 8-bit state quantization and lower effective precision on shorter decode horizons. We implement LoReS in vLLM and demonstrate end-to-end decode speedups.

Machine Learning.title: The (Butter)fly Dream: Linear Separability of World-Model Rollouts in a Connectome-Constrained Visual Model
Machine Learning.summary:
arXiv:2611.01866v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Zhuangzi dreamt he was a butterfly and, on waking, could not tell which was the dream. We ask a version of his question of a model of the fly brain: placed inside a world generated by a world model, can a fixed brain tell that the world is a dream? We treat it as a question about what a connectome-constrained model trained on one task makes available beyond that task: do its responses make the defects of a dream linearly decodable? The observer is a published model of the fly visual system trained only for optic-flow estimation; reality is the MPI-Sintel movie on the model's 721-column retina; dreams are continuations of five real frames by three small world models (a persistence random walk, an MDN-RNN and an RSSM) at three temperatures. The judge is a classifier two-sample test on temporal statistics of cell-type responses, with sequence-level cross-validation. In the trained observer's responses all nine dreams are separable from reality (AUC 0.85-0.99, mean over 50 trained models), in those of the same network before training much less so (0.58-0.75 for the learned world models; paired difference 0.20-0.37), equally on sequences the observer never saw, and in an order unrelated to pixel error. Because these AUCs are near ceiling, we add graded probes made of each window's own real frames with only their order broken. Swapping one adjacent pair of the 14 generated frames gives 0.73 on the trained responses against 0.54 before training and 0.56 for pixel statistics; the trained curve reaches 0.75 at 1.1 swapped pairs of seven, the pixel statistics at 4.7, and the untrained network not at all. A detection horizon, the test on the first k generated frames, orders the world models where the full-length AUC saturates.

Machine Learning.title: A Self-Generated Floor on Adam's $\varepsilon$: Evidence from Power-Law Matrix Sensing
Machine Learning.summary:
arXiv:2611.01868v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: In nonconvex Burer--Monteiro low-rank matrix sensing of $U^\ast \in \mathbb{R}^{V \times D}$ under power-law covariance $\Sigma = \mathrm{diag}(j^{-s})_{j=1}^V$, the precision-wall approximation predicts that Adam stalls when the smallest non-gauge Hessian eigenvalue drops below its denominator floor, giving $s^\ast(V,D) = [\log(1/\varepsilon_{\mathrm{eff}}) - \log V]/\log(VD) + \delta_{\mathrm{Adam}}$. If $\varepsilon_{\mathrm{eff}}$ were set by $\varepsilon_0$, lowering $\varepsilon_0$ from $10^{-10}$ to $10^{-12}$ would raise $s^\ast$ by $0.95\text{--}1.33$. Instead, across six values of $\varepsilon_0$ two decades apart, $10^{-2}$ to $10^{-12}$, the boundary follows the $\varepsilon_0$ slope down to $10^{-6}$, bends near $10^{-8}$, and is flat below $10^{-8}$, while warm-started L-BFGS and Gauss--Newton reach machine precision on stalled instances. We trace this saturation to a self-generated dynamical floor $\varepsilon_{\mathrm{dyn}} \propto \alpha$: high-curvature modes oscillate persistently near the adaptive edge of stability with amplitude $\propto \alpha(1-\beta_1)/(1+\beta_1)$ and leak gradient fluctuations of scale $\kappa\alpha$ into rare modes via measurement coupling, pinning $\sqrt{\hat{v}_V} \approx \kappa\alpha \gg \varepsilon_0$. Fitting a single threshold-crossing wall parameter $\varepsilon_{\mathrm{dyn}} = 4.76\times 10^{-9}$ (with the detection lag frozen at its companion calibration) predicts the saturated failure boundary for $D \ge 4$ across five $(V,D)$ scales to RMS $0.098$ (breaking down at $D = 2$), while shrinking $\varepsilon_0$ below $10^{-8}$ is ineffective and lowering the step size $\alpha$ reduces the floor directly.

Machine Learning.title: Robust Remote ECG Monitoring under Energy Constraints: Anomaly Filtering versus Predictive Uncertainty
Machine Learning.summary:
arXiv:2611.01898v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Machine learning for remote electrocardiogram monitoring must handle noise and diseases absent from training under tight resource constraints. We investigate whether upstream unsupervised anomaly detection can improve monitoring decisions more efficiently than classifier-derived uncertainty. We evaluate five detectors on PTB-XL and BUT QDB and compare a two-stage filter-classifier system with Monte Carlo Dropout and deep ensembles under unseen-disease and noise conditions. Performance is averaged over five training seeds. We measure single-pass energy, latency, and graph memory on a microcontroller's central processing unit (CPU) and neural processing unit (NPU). Per-score neural network costs account for repeated evaluations but exclude scoring outside deployed graphs. Energy equations relate filtering and rejection to avoided classifier execution. Across four disease scenarios, Deep Support Vector Data Description (Deep SVDD) achieves the highest mean area under the receiver operating characteristic curve within all tested finite CPU energy budgets. On the NPU, it leads at 1 mJ, while Monte Carlo Dropout has slightly higher means at 10 and 100 mJ. With a narrow CPU classifier, the Deep SVDD two-stage system increases the fraction of correctly classified or correctly rejected inputs by 15.0-19.4 percentage points over classification without rejection. Estimated energy per input is 1.93-6.99 mJ, compared with 52.53 mJ for Monte Carlo Dropout and 8.76-17.51 mJ for deep ensembles, at each method's retrospectively selected test accuracy peak. These results support upstream filtering for efficient remote monitoring, while independent validation and complete-system measurements remain necessary.

Machine Learning.title: Machine Learning Beyond Statistical Consistency for Hybrid AI
Machine Learning.summary:
arXiv:2611.01914v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: We propose a new definition of machine learning, according to which a machine learns a function when it computes the function successfully, that is, when the value it returns for each input has a proper derivation in a formal system. We extend G\"odel's Representability Theorem, which equates computation with derivation, to empirical targets in two ways: the theorem is extended to the computable reals, and the data are admitted into the system as empirical definitions that record what has been observed. We prove that a machine learns a true probability if and only if two conditions are met. The Truth Condition is that its estimate converges to the true probability, which is statistical consistency. The Assurance Condition is that the machine properly derives its own convergence inside the system. Learning thus lies beyond statistical consistency, for it requires a derivation of the convergence from the record. A global assumption about the data, such as the i.i.d. assumption, does not supply such a derivation, because it leads only to a circular one, as we show for PAC learning. On the other hand, the two conditions are met for the probability of a sentence over a finite ideal corpus. A real machine can approximate a true probability only if an ideal machine can learn it precisely, that is, only in a domain that meets the two conditions. Modern AI works in such a domain, and we offer this as a clue to its success. Modern AI is hybrid as well, in two senses: First, it performs two kinds of tasks, namely probabilistic ones such as predicting the next word and deductive ones such as proving and coding. Second, it combines two parts of different kinds, a statistical proposer and a deductive verifier, for proving and coding. Our framework explains both senses of hybridity in one formal system.

Machine Learning.title: Watch Your Step: Adam's Margin Maximization Bias Depends on the Learning Rate Schedule
Machine Learning.summary:
arXiv:2611.01929v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: We study the implicit bias of Adam and its similarity to sign gradient descent on homogeneous models in binary classification tasks. Perhaps surprisingly, we uncover that these depend on the learning rate schedule. While previous works studied strongly decaying learning rate schedules $\eta(t)=\mathrm o \left(t^{1/L-1}\right)$, where $L$ is the homogeneity degree, and showed $\ell_\infty$-margin-maximization biases, we focus on the more common complementary regime, including constant and weakly decaying schedules. For a polynomial schedule $t^{\alpha}$ and homogeneity degree $L$, we show that when $\alpha > \frac 1L - \frac12$, Adam has no trajectory-independent margin-maximization bias for deep linear networks (in the KKT sense): first, there is no non-trivial, locally Lipschitz, convex implicit regularizer in this setting, including any squared norm. Second, on width-$1$ networks, the result holds without requiring convexity, implying that any implicit regularizer for wide networks must be trivial when restricted to a width-$1$ network. Nevertheless, we positively characterize the implicit bias in this regime as maximizing a trajectory-dependent weighted-$\ell_2$ margin for any $L$-homogeneous model. The fundamental mechanism behind our results is convergence of Adam's preconditioner to a trajectory-dependent vector, which also allows showing that the limiting parameter direction depends on initialization. In the intermediate regime $\frac 1L - 1 \leq \alpha \leq \frac1L - \frac12$ we prove an $\ell_\infty$ bias, conditional on gradient directional convergence to a full-support vector. Of independent interest, we establish a loss decay rate for full batch Adam on general homogeneous models, whose leading order depends only on the second-moment parameter.

Machine Learning.title: ReWY: Faster Gradient Computation for Delta-Rule Attention Family
Machine Learning.summary:
arXiv:2611.01940v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Delta-rule linear attention underlies language models such as Kimi Linear and Qwen3-Next. Chunkwise implementations expose matrix parallelism, but their backward passes compute unnecessary auxiliary adjoints. We present ReWY, an algebraic reformulation that reduces this work before optimizing accelerator execution. Differentiating the chunk correction as one triangular residual system eliminates the inverse adjoint and reduces seven local WY matrix products to three. Two complementary transformations expose further reuse: centered matrix contractions replace pairwise vector-gate processing, and scalar-gate reductions reuse key-gradient products instead of forming a key Gram matrix. These identities simplify backward computation for DeltaNet, GDN, KDA, and GDN2 while preserving the recurrence and gradients in exact arithmetic, without changing the architecture or training objective.
  We implement the reduced graph on GPUs and Ascend NPUs. Under matched recomputation and full-saving policies, precision-qualified six-shape comparisons with frozen FLA references yield 1.15-1.81$\times$ geometric-mean complete low-level backward speedups on NVIDIA GPUs. All four operators achieve 1.18-1.70$\times$ on H100 and H200 while retaining original FP32 working matrices. A separate public-autograd evaluation on Ascend 950DT, including gradient conversions, yields 1.09-2.89$\times$ under available matched policies. Paired ablations establish further ReWY gains after optimizing the complementary contractions. Complete-gradient checks validate the recorded operator cases; supplementary full-model backward measurements assess integration into community FLA models and a GDN2 layer port. Code and reproduction materials: https://github.com/flashserve/ReWY.

Machine Learning.title: OC-OPD: Observation-coordinated Supervision for On-Policy Distillation
Machine Learning.summary:
arXiv:2611.01965v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Reverse and forward Kullback--Leibler (KL) divergences provide complementary supervision in on-policy distillation: reverse KL refines the student's active token rankings, and forward KL allocates mass to teacher-supported candidates. At student-generated prefixes, we form a four-observation matrix by treating the student and teacher as both candidate sources and evaluators. The diagonal self-observations measure uncertainty, while source-centered cross-observations recover the two KL objectives. We establish an exact identity equating the Fisher inverse-metric coupling of their logit gradients with the sum of these contrasts, yielding a common local descent direction for distinct positive distributions. Observation-coordinated on-policy distillation (OC-OPD) uses observations to set preferences, closed-form bargaining to coordinate gradients, and distributional discrepancy to scale the update. Across three heterogeneous student settings (non-thinking generation, thinking generation, and base-model initialization), OC-OPD achieves strong gains in mathematical reasoning and transfers effectively to out-of-distribution scientific question answering and code generation. Our code is publicly available at: https://github.com/RuoranXu/OC-OPD.

Machine Learning.title: Large-Scale Bayesian Optimisation Using Uncertainty-Calibrated Product-of-Experts Gaussian Process Models with Trust Regions
Machine Learning.summary:
arXiv:2611.01984v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: The use of collections of independent local Gaussian processes (GP-ind) combined with trust regions is a widely adopted approach for large-scale and high-dimensional Bayesian optimisation (BO). However, this approach suffers from several limitations, including discontinuities at the boundaries of disjoint regions, an inability to capture long-range spatial correlations, potential information loss, and abrupt increases in computational overhead. To address these limitations, this paper introduces a novel BO algorithm, termed BO-pro-c-tr. The proposed method employs a product-of-experts Gaussian process model with uncertainty calibration (GP-pro-c) as its surrogate model and incorporates a one-to-many association strategy for integrating GP-pro-c with trust regions. Empirical results suggest that, when combined with the GP-LCB acquisition function, BO-pro-c-tr achieves an average reduction of 2.6% in simple regret and 34.9% in computational overhead relative to BO algorithms based on independent local GP models coupled with trust regions.

Machine Learning.title: MIRA: Mutual Information guided calibration for Reliable Test-Time Adaptation
Machine Learning.summary:
arXiv:2611.02003v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Test-time adaptation (TTA) updates a deployed model using only unlabeled target data, but standard entropy-based methods often rely on deterministic confidence and can reinforce overconfident errors under distribution shift. We propose MIRA, Mutual Information guided calibration for Reliable Test-Time Adaptation, a source-free online adaptation method that uses lightweight last-layer Gaussian perturbations to probe prediction reliability. For each target batch, MIRA reuses a single feature extraction pass and samples perturbed classifiers around the source classifier, forming an efficient local predictive distribution. Rather than fitting a Bayesian posterior, MIRA treats the perturbation scale as a local probing radius and selects a batch-specific scale using mutual information (MI) and prediction agreement. The resulting perturbation-sensitivity signal identifies predictions that are confident and locally stable under classifier perturbations, while suppressing brittle predictions with high stochastic disagreement. MIRA then performs adaptation with an MI-confidence weighted entropy loss, which down-weights perturbation-sensitive or low-confidence samples before they drive entropy minimization. This weighted loss reduces the influence of brittle predictions that can otherwise cause harmful adaptation under distribution shift. The method requires no source data, retraining, model ensembles, or offline posterior fitting, and can be applied as a plug-and-play modification to entropy-minimization TTA. Experiments on distribution-shift benchmarks show improvements in accuracy, calibration, and negative log-likelihood, suggesting that mutual-information-guided perturbation probing and weighted adaptation yield more robust online TTA than deterministic confidence.
Machine Learning.comment: Comments: Accepted at NeurIPS 2026

Machine Learning.title: Uncertainty-Aware 3D Position Reconstruction in CZT Drift-Strip Detectors
Machine Learning.summary:
arXiv:2611.02027v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Accurate three-dimensional interaction-position reconstruction is important for CZT drift-strip detectors, but conventional methods can suffer from degraded performance in challenging detector regions, while learned models provide limited information about prediction reliability. We investigate two uncertainty-aware approaches: deep ensembles of point-estimation networks and simulation-based inference (SBI), which estimates a posterior distribution over interaction position. Both approaches are trained on physics-based simulations and evaluated on both synthetic and experimental data. On synthetic data, uncertainty from both methods correlates with positioning error, with SBI showing a substantially stronger relationship. On experimental measurements, the deep ensemble achieves improved $z$-position resolution, while SBI provides more informative uncertainty estimates that highlight regions of reduced positional information and discrepancies between simulation and the physical detector. These results demonstrate the complementary strengths of ensemble-based reconstruction and posterior inference for uncertainty-aware detector position reconstruction.

Machine Learning.title: SensOFormer: Foundation Models for Particle Accelerators
Machine Learning.summary:
arXiv:2611.02031v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Large-scale scientific facilities, such as particle accelerators, are complex systems composed of thousands of interacting components that must operate collectively to support diagnostics and control, and ensure safe, reliable operation. These facilities rely on extensive sensor networks that generate large volumes of heterogeneous, incomplete, and noisy telemetry, often sampled at different rates across subsystems. In this paper, we adopt the foundation-model paradigm to learn general-purpose sensor representations from historical accelerator data through self-supervised pretraining. We introduce SensOFormer, a denoising masked transformer with a Perceiver-style encoder-decoder architecture designed to handle variable sensor sets, accommodate heterogeneous sampling rates, and learn robust representations from noisy measurements. The model is pretrained on multiple particle-accelerator datasets and transferred to downstream tasks, including missing-data imputation, anomaly detection, cavity identification, and fault identification. Through extensive evaluations and comparisons, we demonstrate that a single self-supervised model can learn reusable representations for diverse operational tasks in large-scale scientific facilities. Project page: https://mahindrautela.github.io/sensoformer.

Machine Learning.title: Scalar Smoothness Is One Point on a Besov Spectrum
Machine Learning.summary:
arXiv:2611.02037v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Studies of neural network generalization and robustness often summarize smoothness with a single number, such as a Lipschitz constant or a Hessian curvature statistic. However, Lipschitz constants summarize global worst-case sensitivity and Hessian statistics summarize local curvature; neither captures how model responses vary with the size, direction, and location of perturbations encountered in real-world deployment. To measure smoothness under these perturbations, we introduce a finite-difference roughness spectrum that profiles model responses across these conditions. Our roughness spectrum generalizes scalar smoothness measures, bringing Lipschitz sensitivity and directional Hessian curvature into a common framework across perturbation scales. We connect this spectrum to classical Besov theory, which describes how a function's variation changes with scale. Our theoretical analysis also proves that a larger output shift can cause less task damage than a smaller one, and that local curvature alone can miss the blocks most vulnerable to finite perturbations. In image classification, Roughness Source Control (RSC) suppresses margin roughness along noise directions and improves noise robustness in a comparison of 80 checkpoints across four model--dataset combinations. In post-training quantization, we identify blocks that need higher precision by measuring task-loss increases from perturbations matched to the size and direction of each block's quantization error. Our mixed-precision allocation achieves lower perplexity than the Hessian-based HAWQ-V2 baseline under the same GPTQ weights and bit budgets in all 14 settings across seven held-out large language models.

Machine Learning.title: ECGJev: Question-Conditioned Option Scoring for 12-Lead ECG Interpretation
Machine Learning.summary:
arXiv:2611.02041v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Clinical interpretation of a 12-lead electrocardiogram (ECG) often requires answering targeted diagnostic questions with clear, quantifiable decisions. We introduce ECGJev, the first ECG framework built on a decision decoder, a pretrained language model trained to return a probability for every listed option. A question-conditioned bridge compresses frozen waveform and spectrogram features into 16 ECG tokens, and a two-stage procedure adapts the bridge and low-rank adapters on the decoder's native option readout using diagnostic labels alone, scoring all options for a question in one forward pass. Evaluated across four ECG benchmarks, ECGJev achieves the highest macro-F1 on CPSC2018 (80.46%), PTB-XL (71.68%) and Chapman (96.86%), and generalizes competitively to the small-sample PTB cohort. Concept probes and perturbation analyses further show that its predictions rely directly on the ECG input, remain stable under option-order and wording variations, and transfer zero-shot to unseen waveform concepts. Our code is available at https://github.com/zhuoyuanli-lab/ECGJev.

Machine Learning.title: METER: Matched-Event Calibration for Short-Event EEG Microstate Transition Analysis
Machine Learning.summary:
arXiv:2611.02045v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Short cognitive events contain unequal and often sparse transition evidence, so raw EEG microstate distances can reflect finite sampling rather than neural reconfiguration. We introduce METER (Matched-Event Transition Estimation against a Reference), a participant-relative framework that separates marginal occupancy from conditional next-state choice and evaluates each event against duration-conditioned events from a fixed participant-specific reference bank. METER-Jump integrates uncertainty in sparse target and reference transition tables, returning a randomized event rank for testing and a continuous standardized coordinate for association analysis. Using a reproducible three-state representation selected by spatial criteria, we evaluated METER with participant-fitted simulations, estimator ablations, map perturbations, and preprocessing sensitivities. Event-level false-positive rates were 0.044-0.056 across four heterogeneous null mechanisms. By contrast, global cutoffs learned under the participant-fitted null and transferred unchanged to other regimes produced false-positive rates from 0.004 under rare transitions to 0.234 under map perturbation; duration-conditioned ranks remained near 0.05. Detection probability was approximately 0.69 with fixed maps but fell to 0.22 after bootstrap-derived map-assignment perturbation. In 4,175 natural-reading events from 18 participants, no linguistic association survived multiplicity correction in the primary 30-ms analysis, although a 20-ms sensitivity changed one within-stream max-$T$ decision. METER therefore calibrates finite-event departures conditional on a defined microstate sequence, while map assignment, filtering, temporal smoothing, and reference construction remain separate sources of measurement uncertainty.

Machine Learning.title: Beliefs in feedback: Factored representations of interacting agents in transformers
Machine Learning.summary:
arXiv:2611.02047v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Complex systems, from ecosystems to brains, are usually modeled as modular components coupled through feedback rather than as indivisible wholes. Can a transformer trained on the joint behavior of a group of interacting agents be understood in the same way? In this work, we develop a computational-mechanics framework to study agents interacting in feedback loops. We formally prove that any joint stochastic process can be presented as resulting from the behavior of agents interacting in feedback, and the resulting process is generated by a hidden Markov model whose Bayesian beliefs factorize into separate components per agent. Furthermore, our experiments show that transformers trained on such feedback sequences make use of this separability, disentangling the beliefs about the underlying factors into separate subspaces of their residual stream. This representation is found to scale linearly (instead of exponentially) with the number of agents. Moreover, interventions show that these representations are causally efficacious, allowing for targeted steering of individual agents' beliefs by selectively inserting counterfactuals. However, coarse-graining the behavior is found to disrupt the factorization, and can force a higher-dimensional representation. Together, the results establish both the dimensional advantage of a factorized representation and the ability of transformers to exploit it, laying the groundwork for investigating traces of compositional predictive architecture in pretrained models.

Machine Learning.title: Same Function, Different Gradients: Evaluating Gradient Reliability under Reparameterization
Machine Learning.summary:
arXiv:2611.02052v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Gradients are no longer used only to train models: Gradient magnitudes are now measurement instruments, used to rank attention heads for pruning, to decide per-example clipping in private training, to allocate adapter rank budgets, and to debug models. Across these workflows, larger gradient magnitudes are taken to mean greater importance. Even for a fixed input--output function, these gradients are computed in one of many possible parameter coordinate systems. For example, attention scores depend on the query and key projections only through the paired product $W_QW_K^\top$. Scaling a head's query projection by $c$ and the corresponding key projection by $1/c$ therefore leaves every output logit unchanged. This change in parameter coordinates rescales the corresponding query and key gradient norms by $1/c$ and $c$, respectively. To test whether gradient-based decisions remain unchanged under these coordinate changes, we introduce Gradient Reliability under Reparameterization (GRR). GRR rewrites a trained model in new parameter coordinates that compute exactly the same function, verifies that predictions are unchanged, and then tests whether the decisions derived from the gradients are unchanged too. Our audits span GLUE classifiers, a ViT on CIFAR-10, GPT-2-medium and GPT-2-large, a 1.1B-parameter Llama-style model on WikiText-2, and six trained LoRA adapters. Empirically, predictions are preserved throughout, but both the gradients and the gradient-based decisions change. Across 66 GLUE attention audits, the median top-3 overlap of raw head-gradient rankings is only $1/3$, and rankings and pruning masks change even under the mildest rescalings we test. In the largest of 14 global-pruning audits, the shifted ranking selects head masks that differ in four of 22 pruned heads and reach $50.92\%$ and $94.84\%$ validation accuracy on one ELECTRA SST-2 model.

Machine Learning.title: Fragility Is Not Reducible to Hardness: Conditional Causal Difficulty for LLMs
Machine Learning.summary:
arXiv:2611.02065v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Large language models show large and seemingly arbitrary performance drops when a task is rewritten in ways that leave its requirements untouched. We recast task difficulty as a causal quantity: the treatment effect of meaning-preserving perturbations on a model. A meaning-preserving rewrite can only be observed to hurt a task the model can already solve, so we place the estimand on the principal stratum where the degradation occurs: the conditional causal difficulty (CCD), the probability that a randomly drawn twin breaks a solvable task. Because harder tasks tend to be more phrasing-sensitive, complexity enters as an effect modifier rather than a confounder, and we residualize it out to obtain complexity-residualized difficulty (CRD); zero for a task exactly as fragile as its complexity predicts, positive for anomalously fragile ones. Current benchmarks do not supply the data CCD requires, so we introduce GlassGSM and GlassMATH, augmenting GSM8K and MATH with twins built from perturbation families, raising fragility on GlassGSM by $\approx 12\times$ over GSM-IC-style distractors on the same problems ($3.7\%\to44.9\%$) while keeping the answer key unchanged. Our predictor Frail learns the per-perturbation break probability and reaches $0.613{\pm}0.023$ of the suite reliability ceiling on GlassGSM and $0.557{\pm}0.023$ on GlassMATH, against $0.171$/$0.401$ for a surface-feature baseline and $0.444$/$0.463$ for supervised baselines such as VAP3, and, at a $5\%$ curation budget on GlassGSM, doubles random recall of fragile items, matching an oracle ranking. Additionally, cross-fitted residualization leaves CRD uncorrelated with the declared proxy in practice.
  Code is available at https://github.com/upwork/Conditional_Causal_Difficulty_for_LLMs

Machine Learning.title: Large Geometry Models Are Priors For Fast Physics Pretraining
Machine Learning.summary:
arXiv:2611.02066v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Language and vision models became data-efficient by pretraining on plentiful unlabelled data; physical field models have such data, over ten million 3D shapes, but geometry pretraining designs its targets rather than deriving them from the physics. Euler-Lagrange geometry pretraining derives them: for attached flow, a shape enters the flow's Euler-Lagrange equation only through coefficients that distance and normal line (the normal up to sign) fix to first order. Their reconstruction error therefore bounds what a representation loses about any field, and fine-tuning on costly simulations need only assemble the global field. We realise it in AREALS, a masked surface autoencoder whose areal tokens carry position, normal and area, pretrained self-supervised and sign-free on 61,822 raw meshes. Because the operating condition enters only through the far field, sensors can supply it: AREALS completes a hidden field in one forward pass without condition labels. It matches the accuracy of the same architecture trained from scratch with half the simulations on DrivAerML and DrivAerNet++ and about a quarter on WindsorML. On DoubleDelta wings, 20 sensors give $3.9\times$ and $4.0\times$ lower field and force error than GABI, a Bayesian inversion method with a learned prior, and beyond the training angles pretraining halves the error.

Machine Learning.title: HQNN-CL: Regime-Aware Hybrid Quantum Neural Network with Continual Learning for Financial Forecasting
Machine Learning.summary:
arXiv:2611.02091v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Financial time-series forecasting is still difficult owing to the non-stationary nature of the market, regime changes, and catastrophic forgetting, which makes conventional deep learning models hard to adapt in the long term. To achieve uncertainty-aware robust financial forecasting in the face of changing market conditions, this study proposes a Hybrid Quantum-Classical Neural Network with Continual Learning (HQNN-CL). The proposed framework combines Gaussian Hidden Markov Model (HMM) based regime detection, BiLSTM temporal encoding, adaptive-depth parameterized quantum circuits, Elastic Weight Consolidation (EWC), experience replay, and probabilistic forecasting in a single architecture. The framework was tested on four real-time stock datasets: Microsoft, Systems Limited, Teradata and Tata Consultancy Services, and compared with seven state-of-the-art forecasting models, including recurrent and Transformer-based models. The experimental results show that HQNN-CL has outperformed other methods on the Systems Limited (RMSE = 3.0149) and Teradata (RMSE = 0.8909) datasets and is within 0.32% and 0.40% of the best baseline method for Microsoft and Tata Consultancy Services, respectively. The proposed framework also generates well-calibrated probabilistic forecasts within the range of 89.5% to 96.5% empirical coverage rate, has zero catastrophic forgetting (BWT = 0.0000) for all sequential learning tasks, and consistently shows positive forward transfer. Ablation and statistical significance analyses also validate the performance of adaptive quantum feature learning and continual adaptation under heterogeneous market conditions, regime-wise.

Machine Learning.title: Bernoulli On-Policy Distillation: Don't Ignore High-Confidence Student Tokens
Machine Learning.summary:
arXiv:2611.02093v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: On-policy distillation (OPD) trains a student language model on its own trajectories using token-level supervision from a stronger teacher. We show that standard sampled reverse-KL OPD systematically suppresses updates to high-confidence tokens, such that their weak gradient contribution does not necessarily imply weak or uninformative teacher supervision. We introduce Bernoulli On-Policy Distillation (Bernoulli OPD), which directly matches the teacher and student probabilities for that token. This yields a bounded probability space correction that preserves teacher-student disagreement while avoiding the additional confidence-dependent suppression induced by vanilla OPD. Fixed-rollout analyses show that Bernoulli OPD substantially restores optimization signal to high-confidence tokens while remaining sensitive to teacher-student disagreement. We further analyze the resulting model behavior through confidence distributions, answer calibration, policy movement, and training dynamics, showing that Bernoulli OPD's gains cannot be explained simply by longer reasoning, larger optimization steps, or more uniform imitation of the teacher. Code is available at https://github.com/duterscmy/Bernoulli-OPD.

Machine Learning.title: NorthCUA Technical Report: Turbocharging Computer-Use Agents through Experience at Scale
Machine Learning.summary:
arXiv:2611.02102v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Scaling computer-use agents from individual actions to complex software work requires experience that connects decisions to complete outcomes. We present NorthCUA, an integrated system for turbocharging computer-use agents through experience at scale. Its Experience Flywheel supplies diverse executable tasks to the NorthCUA Harness, which sustains long interactions, records decisions, and checks task outcomes. The Flywheel uses these records to curate verified trajectories. For unsolved tasks, recursive self-improvement evolves reusable skills and preserves verified milestones so later attempts build on earlier progress. Staged Learning combines this experience with grounding data from the Flywheel to develop GUI competence through mid-training and long-horizon supervised fine-tuning. The policy then learns from fresh attempts in the same Harness through joint desktop-web reinforcement learning, closing the loop between experience production and policy improvement. The resulting Nano, Mini, and Pro family achieves state-of-the-art results among open-source models across GUI grounding, desktop execution, and Web interaction under the reported evaluation settings. For more responsive Web workflows, NorthCUA-Ultrafast pairs direct action selection with open-ended generation on pre-RL Nano, offering a measured quality-latency tradeoff. Together, these advances establish NorthCUA as a high-performing model family and a reusable foundation for agents that carry complex software work from intent to completion.

Machine Learning.title: Order-Only On-Policy Distillation
Machine Learning.summary:
arXiv:2611.02112v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: On-policy distillation (OPD) trains a student on its own generations by matching the teacher's token probabilities. These probabilities entangle two kinds of information: which tokens the teacher prefers, and how confident it is. The latter reflects the teacher's own capacity and calibration, which a smaller student may be unable to reproduce. Because the teacher temperature changes these values without changing the ordering, OPD is also sensitive to the temperature choice. We ask whether the teacher's ordering of candidate tokens is enough, and propose Order-Only On-Policy Distillation (O$^{3}$PD). At each student-generated prefix, O$^{3}$PD trains the student to reproduce the order of the teacher's top-$K$ tokens, without fitting their probability values. The objective is therefore invariant to the teacher temperature and needs no temperature tuning. Across six teacher--student pairs, O$^{3}$PD outperforms OPD on the average over HMMT25, AIME24, and AIME25 in every pair, by up to 2.9 points, with gains of up to 5.6 points on AIME25. Other ranking losses yield similar gains, so the benefit comes from ordinal supervision itself. Analysis shows that O$^{3}$PD departs further from the teacher's probabilities than OPD, yet reproduces its ranking more faithfully and yields a stronger student. The ranking, not the probability values, thus carries the knowledge that on-policy distillation needs to transfer.

Machine Learning.title: Conditional Calibration Contracts under Coupled Load: A Branch-Aware Audit of Switched Inference
Machine Learning.summary:
arXiv:2611.02121v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Bursty serving changes both queue states and the population selected for each model. We study conditional calibration contracts as a specification to be validated, rather than a certified property of an existing router. CA-MHD combines load-coupled distillation, closed-loop replay and a cost-informed Schmitt router in a discrete-event simulator with a hardware service table. Across 40 cells (ten training seeds and four content-load coupling levels), we distinguish the original teacher, frozen wide heads on an adapted trunk, and the narrow student. A common teacher-trajectory audit has median absolute student-teacher deficit 0.06 percentage points, but does not certify the student-selected deployment support. Historical results use a kernel correctness gap, not the published SmoothECE; we separately prove selected-branch composition for a residual functional at a common fixed scale. The deployed wide branch has lower ordinal accuracy than the original teacher in all 40 cells. Same-checkpoint student-only serving has lower historical ordinal gap in 27/40 cells; routing also exposes violation tails up to 17.5 percent. Student p99 latency remains above the 1.5 ms target. Retrospective temporal recalibration improves the ordinal gap in 39/40 cells, but causal delayed-label availability is unverified and no incremental per-mode benefit is detected after multiplicity adjustment. An in-sample CUSUM detects 30/40 checkpoint changes at five historical false alarms, with no prospective false-alarm guarantee. These findings support a branch-aware audit and a scoped negative result, not demonstrated routing superiority. Independent budgets, selected-support validation and net utility under a satisfied SLA remain open.

Machine Learning.title: Mesh2Shell Neural Operator for Inverse Shape Optimization
Machine Learning.summary:
arXiv:2611.02127v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Physics-driven design seeks high-performing geometries, which need not conform to a learned shape category. Parametric and latent-space approaches facilitate surrogate-based optimization, but restrict deformations to prescribed shape families or learned decoders. We introduce the Mesh-to-Shell Neural Operator (M2S-NO) as the mesh-to-shell component of a category-agnostic inverse shape optimization framework. We separate the explicit mesh used for design from the volumetric representation used for physics prediction. M2S-NO maps oriented surface samples to a surface-centered shell representation, such as TruncatedSDF or HeatSDF. A separate problem-specific PDE neural operator (PDE-NO) maps this representation to physical fields. Objective gradients update mesh vertices through both operators, without a latent shape decoder. Preconditioning and remeshing support free-form deformation, while fixed interfaces are controlled directly on the mesh. Optional shell-space proposals enable topology changes. We evaluate geometric matching, jet-engine brackets, and neutron moderators, with independent FEM and OpenMC evaluation. Relative to the best training designs, M2S-NO reduces maximum bracket displacement by 14.3% and increases neutron-sensor current by 13.8%. Optimization also succeeds from an out-of-distribution bracket initialization, demonstrating the framework's geometric flexibility.

Machine Learning.title: TSSDA: An Autonomous Agent for Constructing a Time-Series Text-to-SQL Benchmark
Machine Learning.summary:
arXiv:2611.02132v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: As agents increasingly undertake data querying, Text-to-SQL serves as a foundational capability for database access. However, for text-to-SQL in time-series databases, high-quality benchmarks and large-scale training corpora remain scarce, limiting the systematic evaluation and domain adaptation of existing models and agents. Existing automated SQL generation approaches lack sufficient autonomy, leaving key challenges unresolved. First, numerous combinations of temporal syntax and functions complicate comprehensive coverage of valid queries. Second, as the corpus grows, generating valuable and diverse new data becomes increasingly challenging. Third, schema and data heterogeneity hinder reuse of temporal query structures, limiting generation efficiency. To address these challenges, we propose TSSDA, a Time-Series SQL (TSSQL) Generation Data Agent framework, and construct TERN, a comprehensive Time-sERies text-to-SQL beNchmark. First, to achieve broad coverage of valid queries, we systematically model TSSQL syntax and semantics to construct a data generation space. Next, to explore the space and improve diversity, we develop a Data Agent that autonomously orchestrates data generation. The agent comprises a planning and decision-making module and a query generation module, with online adaptation for continuous self-improvement. Finally, we introduce a temporal-aware memory that enables adaptive reuse of experience across heterogeneous data instances, improving generation efficiency. Comprehensive evaluations on TERN reveal the limitations of existing methods in performing Text-to-TSSQL tasks. Furthermore, extensive experiments demonstrate that TSSDA substantially improves coverage, diversity, and complexity.

Machine Learning.title: When Is Personalized Federated Learning Worth Its Deployment Cost?
Machine Learning.summary:
arXiv:2611.02146v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Personalized federated learning (PFL) may improve client-level performance, but deeper personalization increases deployment cost. We formulate personalization-depth selection as a utility-based empirical decision problem in which client utility equals Macro-F1 minus a cost-sensitivity weight times deployment cost, over six personalization depths labeled P0 through P5. We compare fixed policies with an offline per-client Oracle reference and report allocation maps over Dirichlet data heterogeneity and cost sensitivity. Although evaluated on this hierarchy, the formulation can accommodate any finite candidate set. On CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and a PTB-XL subset, personalization shows empirical, setting-dependent decision regimes rather than a universal benefit: higher cost sensitivity shifts Oracle mass toward the global-only depth P0; low cost sensitivity can favor deeper actions. Patterns are grid observations (three seeds per cell), not theoretical boundaries. Best-uniform is competitive with Oracle assignment (6.5 percent plus or minus 7.8 percent relative regret; 95 percent confidence interval 5.9 to 7.1), whereas random and personalize-all incur much larger regret (189.3 percent plus or minus 367.1 percent and 409.0 percent plus or minus 803.2 percent). Under the same utility, Ditto full-model personalization is substantially suboptimal once cost is counted. The contribution is an offline characterization of when personalization depth is worth its cost, not a new PFL optimizer or deployment-time scheduler.

Machine Learning.title: Value Forcing: Aligning Return Distributions at All Noise Levels
Machine Learning.summary:
arXiv:2611.02160v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Learning accurate value functions is central to reinforcement learning (RL), yet remains challenging because supervision is limited and indirect: ground-truth values are unavailable, and each transition in the data only provides an immediate reward that can be used to construct bootstrapped targets as supervision. This challenge is particularly pronounced when data is limited or reward signals are sparse, as is common in real-world applications such as robotics. We argue that the key to accurate value learning in this limited data regime is extracting richer learning signals from the available data. In this paper, we introduce Value Forcing, a new approach that uses flow matching to estimate return distributions and enables accurate value learning from limited data. Our key insight is that we can extract richer learning signals by enforcing Bellman consistency at every noise level. Empirically, Value Forcing improves the accuracy of estimating the return distribution, and prevents the distribution from collapsing to a single value, as occurs with prior methods. We instantiate Value Forcing with two practical value-learning algorithms: VF, an actor-critic method, and IVF, an implicit value-learning method. We evaluate both algorithms across $26$ long-horizon tasks in the offline RL setting and find that they outperform prior value-learning methods, with particularly large gains when data is limited. Our project website is available at https://chongyi-zheng.github.io/value-forcing.

Machine Learning.title: Restrained Diffusion Bridges: Targeted Denoiser Training and Refinement
Machine Learning.summary:
arXiv:2611.02170v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Diffusion models are often inaccurate in critical, data-sparse regions of the target distribution. Sampling from restrained distributions, biased distributions used in classical enhanced sampling to concentrate data near chosen configurations, can control where training data are collected but biases the learned distribution. We establish that this bias cancels exactly when forward noising from restrained data is conditioned on the restrained configuration at an appropriately chosen intermediate time. This allows a pretrained model fine-tuned on restrained data to achieve high accuracy in any chosen region of the target distribution, regardless of its probability, using standard denoising or flow matching objectives without importance weights. When no target data are available, Gibbs sampling enables inference from a model trained exclusively on restrained data.

Machine Learning.title: Beyond Unit-Circle Eigenvalues: Invariant Bases for Stable State Space Dynamics
Machine Learning.summary:
arXiv:2611.02174v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Diagonal state space models process long sequences at linear cost, yet the same transition is applied at every step of a rollout, so an unconstrained recurrence holds no quantity fixed and the state decays or grows without bound. Current designs constrain one quantity, and preserving one does not guarantee preservation of the others, so a model can hold its norm to machine precision while momentum drifts by hundreds of percent. We claim that the conserved quantities of a diagonal recurrence are layered, that each layer requires a strictly stronger condition on the operator, and that a unit-modulus spectrum reaches only the outermost. Acting on the claim, we enforce the conditions required for every layer by construction. The generator of the Kronecker-Cayley transition (KC) is a graph Laplacian over object subspaces, $\mathbf{H}=\mathbf{L}\otimes I_m$, advanced by a Cayley transform, and the step stays diagonal at $O(N^3+N^2m)$ cost. The conserved set is exactly a $2m^2$-dimensional family of quadratic forms, held at every parameter value, so the quantities and the dynamics the construction reaches are fixed before training. On four conservation benchmarks, KC holds total mass at or near the reference floor while every diagonal baseline loses it by orders of magnitude. We further compare against mass correction and find that two correctors fail once the underlying prediction diverges, which shows that assembly rather than correction is necessary for a guarantee that holds across the rollout. A free modal basis trained under a conservation penalty conserves only by freezing its spectrum, whereas the assembled operator conserves with every mode but one free to rotate. Beyond these benchmarks, KC holds the linear momentum of three $N$-body systems and, at the operator level, the conserved quantity in molecular dynamics, chemical kinetics, pharmacokinetics and power-grid swing dynamics.
Machine Learning.comment: Comments: Accepted at NeurIPS 2026. 40 pages, 13 figures, 27 tables. Code: this https URL

Machine Learning.title: ANCHOR: KL-Anchored Adaptation for Stable Offline-to-Online RL
Machine Learning.summary:
arXiv:2611.02177v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Offline-to-online reinforcement learning (RL) follows the pretrain-finetune paradigm: an agent is first pretrained on historical data and then adapted through online interaction. We study offline-to-online adaptation without offline replay, where the agent must improve using only the pretrained model and newly collected experience. A key challenge is to avoid catastrophic failure, a sharp early performance collapse during online fine-tuning, while still achieving strong asymptotic performance. Through controlled experiments, we show that removing offline replay can induce catastrophic failure, while retaining strong conservative regularization from offline RL can suppress final online performance. We also find that common stabilization strategies do not reliably prevent early collapse, and that the critic-side mechanisms we test are insufficient on their own. Motivated by these findings, we propose ANCHOR, a simple adaptation method that anchors the actor to the offline-pretrained policy early in online fine-tuning, anneals this constraint over time, and retains only a small residual conservative critic regularizer. We provide a theoretical interpretation showing that KL anchoring helps preserve critic reliability across nearby occupancy distributions, with a two-phase regret bound explaining when anchoring should be maintained or relaxed. Across FrankaKitchen, AntMaze, and Adroit tasks, ANCHOR substantially reduces catastrophic failure while maintaining strong asymptotic performance. Ablations show that KL annealing and the residual conservative weight are important for balancing early stability and online adaptation, while additional analysis shows that ANCHOR is most beneficial when the pretrained policy contains useful behavior to preserve. Code is available at https://github.com/Cho-Geonwoo/ANCHOR.

Machine Learning.title: Fuzzy-Enhanced Machine Learning Approach for Type 2 Diabetes Diagnosis
Machine Learning.summary:
arXiv:2611.02188v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Accurate diabetes prediction is critical for early clinical intervention, yet existing machine-learning pipelines often fail due to class imbalance, noisy physiological measurements, and redundant or weakly informative features. To address these unresolved limitations, this study establishes a unified fuzzy-evolutionary-ensemble framework designed to uncover a more discriminative feature space for type 2 diabetes prediction. The workflow integrates selective fuzzification of nonlinear clinical variables, SMOTE-ENN-based balancing and noise filtering, and Bat-Algorithm-driven evolutionary feature selection prior to training a Random Forest classifier. Applied to the Pima Indians Diabetes Dataset, the framework compresses the expanded fuzzy-numerical space into an optimized 10-feature subset and yields substantial performance gains: 96.11% accuracy, 95.14% precision, 98.00% recall, and a 98.23% F1-score. Relative to a baseline Random Forest using all 16 features (74.45% accuracy; 59.86% F1), the system achieves more than a 1.6-fold improvement in F1-score while preserving over 99% stability in majority-class detection and surpassing earlier published 16-feature models impacted by imbalance and weak feature relevance. Collectively, these results demonstrate that the integrated pipeline produces an enhanced fuzzy-numerical representation space that improves diabetes risk stratification and provides a scalable, uncertainty-aware foundation for diagnostic modeling across broader clinical datasets.

Machine Learning.title: Test-Time Scaling for Open-Ended Reasoning at Small Model Scale
Machine Learning.summary:
arXiv:2611.02208v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: A vote over a model's samples can only help when the samples disagree. For open-ended generation the binding question is therefore not how to combine samples but whether a model produces samples worth combining, a question test-time scaling has answered for math but not for free-form text. We study it at small scale with semantic cluster voting, a judge-free aggregator that groups a small instruct model's samples by meaning and returns the largest cluster's representative, with no reward model or self-judging. On a 250-prompt benchmark with three tiers of answer checkability, the same pattern holds across three model families (Qwen2.5-3B, Llama-3.2-3B, Gemma-2-2B) and two generation seeds: voting raises accuracy on the math control, where samples vary but stay checkable (a gain of +10 to +29 points across the three models), yet adds at most +0.30 judge points on open-ended text. On a larger 200-problem MATH-500 run with the primary model, the math gain is +8.5 points (95% CI [+4.0, +13.0]). Almost every open-ended sample falls into one meaning cluster, so there is little to select over. The collapse is consistent with instruction-tuning rather than model size, and raising decoding temperature does not recover usable diversity, because it costs more quality than it adds (net -0.64 judge points, 95% CI [-0.93, -0.37]).

Machine Learning.title: Discrimination, Calibration, and Ranking: A Unified Matrix Framework
Machine Learning.summary:
arXiv:2611.02215v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Discrimination, calibration, and ranking are the three pillars of classifier evaluation, yet no single algebraic language spans all three. A recent indicator-matrix account unifies discrimination measures (precision, recall, F1, Matthews correlation) across binary, multiclass, multilabel and related settings, using Boolean cell operations on indicator label matrices, generalised to soft labels by t-norms. Calibration measures (Brier score, log-loss) and ranking measures (nDCG, AUC) fall outside it. We close the gap with two further classes of cell operators: deviation operators phi(y - yhat), which give a Calibration Framework, and rank- and slice-dependent operators (positional gains for DCG, column concordance cells for AUC), which give a Ranking Framework. Both inherit the micro/macro/exemplar aggregation architecture. For calibration, the three Brier aggregations collapse to one scalar; the Murphy decomposition holds in matrix form (unbinned, binned and isotonic); and, within the Brier-type class-indexed family, a measure is skew-invariant if and only if it depends only on the class-conditional errors alpha_j and beta_j, the calibration analogues of recall and specificity. For ranking, raw DCG collapses across aggregations while nDCG does not; per-class nDCG and per-class AUC are related by a row-column duality; micro-AUC differs from pooled ROC-AUC; raw positional scores are never strictly proper, and nDCG and AUC need not be proper. The skew-invariant per-class building blocks share one class-conditional expectation template. Experiments on two multilabel benchmarks illustrate the distinctions. Many of the results are machine-checked in Lean 4; the proofs, the experiments and the aggmetrics.scores package are public: https://github.com/rcprati/discrimination-calibration-ranking

Machine Learning.title: Who Should Score the Cache? Mid-Depth Layers Are the Best Judges of KV-Cache Eviction
Machine Learning.summary:
arXiv:2611.02230v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Key-value (KV) cache eviction methods rank tokens by attention scores, and each layer scores its own cache. To our knowledge, no eviction method asks which layer should score. We find, across twenty-one models, that the depth of the scoring layer governs eviction quality. On the eighteen models with per-layer caches, spanning 0.5B to 109B, long-context retrieval accuracy collapses at shallow layers, peaks between 0.4 and 0.75 of depth, and degrades at the last layer. The curve arises because a layer judges tokens well only once it has used the question to find the answer, which takes several layers. Modeling eviction as a top-$k$ cut, we compute answer survival probability from prefill attention and reproduce the measured curves. This approach selects the scoring layer using calibration prompts with known answers, and the selected layer is the best layer measured on most models and never significantly below it. It improves on the own-layer default on sixteen of the eighteen models, with significant gains on seven, all at 14B or below, while on larger models the default is already close to the best mid-depth layer. Scoring every cache from the selected layer while keeping one set of tokens for all heads also beats per-head SnapKV by 18 to 43 points on five models up to 14B under tight budgets. This gain carries over to financial filings at 32K context, all at the same memory budget, with no extra forward pass. The same curve explains a penalty in shared-cache models, where several layers read one cache and the layer that writes it scores by default. On Gemma-4-E2B the writer is shallow and loses 28 points to a mid-depth reader at a 10% budget. We also find that in open-book question answering (LongBench) no mid-depth layer beats the own-layer default.

Machine Learning.title: Iterative Gumbel Planning for Continuous Control
Machine Learning.summary:
arXiv:2611.02236v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Search-based planning remains a powerful policy improvement paradigm in reinforcement learning, driving milestone successes in discrete domains. However, extending this paradigm to continuous control exposes a structural mismatch: search evaluates a finite set of action candidates, whereas continuous RL typically relies on Gaussian policies. We show that winner-action distillation into a continuous Gaussian induces a \textit{projection error} and a stepwise variance-expanding gradient tendency when the selected action is sufficiently far from the current mean. Empirically, this tendency is associated with elevated terminal variance and a return gap on the evaluated tasks. To address this, we propose \textbf{Iterative Gumbel Planning (IGP)}. By adopting a per-dimension factorized categorical policy, IGP naturally aligns the policy support with the search candidates, eliminating the projection error and reducing the residual approximation to a bounded discretization error. To bypass the combinatorial explosion of high-dimensional discrete action spaces, IGP pairs Gumbel Top-$K$ candidate sampling with an MPPI-style multi-round iterative search to refine the policy at each state. Empirically, IGP achieves state-of-the-art aggregate performance and sample efficiency on DMControl and HumanoidBench. Furthermore, it produces more stable action sequences with lower temporal variance, demonstrating its practical potential for real-world robotic deployment.

Machine Learning.title: Nonreciprocal Spherical Attention and Retrieval: Sharp Coarsening Clocks and Certified Score Correction
Machine Learning.summary:
arXiv:2611.02237v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: We develop nonreciprocal spherical attention as a mathematical framework for coarsening and compressed nearest-neighbor retrieval. For two shrinking acute blocks whose centers have zero skew pairing and whose total mass ratio is subexponential in inverse temperature, we prove $\lim_{\beta\to\infty}\beta^{-1}\log T_\beta=1-\cos\phi$, without restricting particle-count growth. An explicit three-body flow has two rigorously separated metastable exponents. For finite compression, mass centering yields a sharp $O(r^2)$ attention-output error bound at fixed temperature, with an explicit spherical-normalization correction. We formulate skew query-side score calibration as a strictly convex moment problem and derive a unique normal equation, residual-based optimization certificates, and bounded low-rank projections. A norm-aware margin objective calibrates native squared-distance rankings. Experiments use semantic retrieval data, one million visual descriptors with three codebook seeds, and a ten-million-vector FAISS IVF-PQ index with recomputed exact cosine ground truth. On SIFT1M, skew margin calibration raises native-L2 hit@10 from 0.8926 to 0.8948; symmetric calibration reaches 0.8996. The ten-million-vector index reaches 0.8827 hit@10 at 0.1794 ms per query in a four-thread batch benchmark, while validation selects no skew update. Exact streamed attention over ten million keys evaluates compressed memory on 1,024 held-out queries. Independent matrix solves, automatic differentiation, finite differences, interval arithmetic, full-flow tests, and nine Rocq-checked algebra lemmas support reproducibility. Directionality alone does not establish retrieval superiority.

Machine Learning.title: Metamorphic Testing for Evaluating Robustness of Sentiment Analysis Models
Machine Learning.summary:
arXiv:2611.02248v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Machine learning systems are challenging to test using traditional software testing methods because their behavior is learned from data rather than explicitly programmed. This challenge is particularly significant in natural language processing (NLP), where small input variations can lead to unexpected model behavior. Conventional evaluation metrics, such as accuracy and F1-score, often fail to capture such inconsistencies. Metamorphic testing addresses this limitation by evaluating expected relationships between original and transformed inputs. With the increasing prevalence of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) and language-based AI systems, the need for systematic robustness testing has become even more pronounced. Motivated by this growing need, this paper presents a lightweight, batch-based metamorphic testing approach for evaluating the robustness of such systems. In particular, we consider sentiment analysis as a representative NLP task and evaluate a pretrained classifier under four transformations: synonym replacement, typo injection, word-order variation, and negation. Using consistency score, flip accuracy, and confidence change, we identify strengths in handling semantic variations and vulnerabilities to textual noise and logical transformations. These findings highlight the value of metamorphic testing in identifying behavioral inconsistencies beyond conventional performance metrics and demonstrate its potential as a systematic framework for evaluating the robustness of language-based AI systems and guiding performance improvements before deployment.

Machine Learning.title: Retrain, Alert, or Rollback? A Three-Response Decision Framework for Production ML Under Concept Drift
Machine Learning.summary:
arXiv:2611.02251v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: When a deployed model degrades under concept drift, an operator can retrain it, raise an alert and monitor, or roll back. Yet most drift-adaptation methods consider only retraining. We present RAR (Retrain-Alert-Rollback), a state machine that gives each response an explicit trigger and cost. Retraining is gated on drift detection, label availability, and measured degradation.
