Machine Learning.title: DTA-GT: Direction- and Topology-Aware Graph Transformer for Neural Network Representation Learning
Machine Learning.summary:
arXiv:2610.16822v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Architecture attribute predictors reduce the cost of neural architecture search by estimating accuracy or latency from a small set of evaluated candidates. Neural architectures are operation-labeled directed acyclic graphs (DAGs), where edge directions determine computational roles and execution dependencies. Existing graph Transformer predictors incorporate topological and directional information in different ways, but primarily focus on specific mechanisms rather than coordinated encoder-wide modeling of these semantics. We introduce encoder-wide directional consistency, a design principle that coordinates the modeling of directed computational semantics across node initialization, global spectral encoding, pairwise interaction, and feature updates. To implement this principle, we propose DTA-GT, a Direction- and Topology-Aware Graph Transformer that integrates direction- and topology-aware node initialization, Magnetic Laplacian spectral encoding, direction-dual structural attention, and a Direction-Sensitive MoE-FFN. Across accuracy and latency prediction on NAS-Bench-101 and NAS-Bench-201, DTA-GT consistently outperforms representative sequence-, GNN-, Transformer-, and hybrid predictors under limited-budget settings. Ablations and Magnetic spectral controls support the contribution of the direction-aware stages and orientation-sensitive spectral information, while mechanistic diagnostics characterize module behavior. These results support encoder-wide directional consistency as an effective design principle for architecture DAG representation.

Machine Learning.title: Revisiting the 16x Pretraining Compute Gap between Diffusion and Autoregressive Language Models
Machine Learning.summary:
arXiv:2610.17590v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Diffusion language models (DLMs) have attracted wide attention for their fast, parallel decoding, but they are believed to be far less efficient to train than autoregressive language models (ARMs): a widely cited study reports that a DLM needs roughly 16x the training compute of an ARM to match its likelihood, a figure that has made pretraining DLMs from scratch look prohibitive at scale. We find that the methodology behind this figure has fallen out of step with current DLM practice: it scores the model with its evidence lower bound (ELBO) and trains a full-sequence, decoder-only model. We therefore revisit the scaling laws of DLMs, adopting the exact likelihood under the model's own decoding order, block diffusion training, an encoder-decoder architecture, and a sweep over the block sizes used in practice. Under this new protocol, we study across ten model variants, about 1,700 models in total, and find that pretraining DLMs is far cheaper than previously thought. Concretely, scoring with the exact likelihood reduces the compute multiple to 12.8x; block diffusion training and an encoder-decoder architecture further reduce it to 7.8x at block size 32, and smaller block sizes narrow it to 4.6x at block size 8 and 3.0x at block size 4. We complement these scaling analyses with an empirical rule for the optimal decoder depth of encoder-decoder block diffusion, a held-out compute budget beyond the fitting range at which the gap between variants persists, and downstream benchmark results where likelihood improvements carry over to accuracy. Overall, the 16x figure substantially overstates the pretraining cost gap between DLMs and ARMs, and pretraining DLMs from scratch is far more viable than previously assumed.

Machine Learning.title: Fractional Power-of-Two Quantization for Efficient and Effective Multiplier-Free LLM Inference
Machine Learning.summary:
arXiv:2610.21257v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) demand efficient inference, where the multiply-accumulate (MAC) operations in linear projections dominate compute and energy cost. Post-training quantization (PTQ) reduces this cost by mapping weights and activations to low-bit integers. Power-of-Two (PoT) weight quantization promises efficient multiplier-free LLM inference via shift-add logic, but suffers significant accuracy degradation at low bit-widths due to its coarse base-2 quantization grid. We introduce Fractional PoT (FPoT), a base-$\sqrt{2}$ (half-octave) fractional PoT grid that achieves practical 4-bit weight quantization while preserving a fully integer shift-add datapath. The method combines (i) the base-$\sqrt{2}$ weight grid with uniform integer activations, (ii) a calibration-time grid-alignment refinement absorbed into the static per-channel scale, and (iii) a lightweight 1-adder $\sqrt{2}$ approximation whose error is absorbed during weight calibration via approximate-grid quantization, yielding a processing element (PE) with significantly fewer gates than a 4-bit integer multiplier. On Llama-3-8B with 4-bit weight and activation quantization, FPoT improves zero-shot commonsense reasoning performance by 8.72% relative to the PoT baseline, while maintaining performance close to the uniform integer baseline, with only a negligible 0.4%p degradation. These results hold across various configurations spanning seven models and three bit-widths. Furthermore, FPoT can be integrated with state-of-the-art LLM PTQ methods, demonstrating framework-agnostic applicability.

Machine Learning.title: Sparse Federated Echo State Networks for Time-Series Classification via Smooth-L1 Regularization
Machine Learning.summary:
arXiv:2610.21742v3 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Echo State Networks (ESNs), as lightweight implementations of reservoir computing, provide efficient solutions for temporal data processing in resource-constrained environments. While standard ESNs offer computational efficiency, their dense readout layers inflate the stored model and the per-sample inference cost. This paper introduces a Smooth-L1 regularized ESN (SL1ESN) that promotes sparsity in the readout layer while preserving differentiability for gradient-based optimization. The method employs a twice-differentiable Smooth-L1 approximation compatible with Newton's method, which we exploit both for centralized training and for a second-order (Newton-step) federated aggregation scheme. Under a single fixed shrinkage threshold shared by every dataset and both settings, experiments on seven time-series classification benchmarks show that SL1ESN learns readouts that are 77-95% sparse in the centralized setting and 75-95% sparse in the federated one. On five of the seven benchmarks, the mean accuracy of the sparse readout over ten seeds differs from that of the stronger dense baseline by at most 0.7 points in the centralized setting and 1.6 points in the federated one, differences of the same order as the seed-to-seed variation, while on the remaining two it trails by 2.4-5.8 points. The second-order federated update converges in only a few rounds. The resulting sparsity compresses the stored model, the per-sample inference cost, and the server-to-client broadcast by a comparable factor. These results demonstrate the practical value of sparse readouts for edge computing and IoT deployments.

Machine Learning.title: Interpretable Cutting Plane Selection for Mixed-Integer Linear Programming Using Genetic Programming
Machine Learning.summary:
arXiv:2610.29311v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Cutting planes (cuts) remove fractional solutions from mixed-integer linear programs (MILPs) without excluding any feasible integer solutions, making them a key ingredient in modern MILP solvers. Current state-of-the-art solvers rely on fine-tuned handcrafted cut strategies, which, despite their effectiveness, remain inherently static and can be suboptimal. More recently, learning-based approaches have been proposed to design adaptive cut strategies; however, most of these methods are based on neural networks, offering limited interpretability and providing no guarantees of convergence. In this paper, we propose \emph{Genetic Programming and Statistics-based Cut Selection} (GPSCS), the first learning-based framework that explicitly generalizes handcrafted cut selection heuristics into a fully interpretable policy. First, a genetic programming model evolves a symbolic scoring function that ranks candidate cuts using features derived from the cuts and the solving context. Second, a lightweight statistics-based mechanism adaptively determines the number of top-ranked cuts to add at each separation round by detecting significant score dropouts. We evaluate GPSCS within the SCIP solver on seven classes of synthetic and real-world benchmark instances, with a strong emphasis on generalization: evaluation instances are on average 41 times harder than those used for training. Experimental results show that GPSCS improves average solving time by $6\%$ compared to SCIP's default cut selection strategy and achieves a two-fold speedup over both a recent neural-network-based approach and a no-cut baseline, demonstrating strong robustness and generalization across heterogeneous MILP families.

Machine Learning.title: Trace2World: Reconstructing App Worlds from Real Interaction Traces for Scalable GUI Agent Training
Machine Learning.summary:
arXiv:2610.30792v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Scaling GUI reinforcement learning requires environments that preserve real-app behavior. Yet coupling behavior inference with coding can turn partial traces into runnable mocks with incorrect state transitions. We introduce \textbf{Trace2World}, which separates global behavior reconstruction from implementation. It reconciles traces into a shared, source-linked app model, then compiles an executable environment. Independent replay of source workflows localizes mismatches for bounded implementation repair. Validated worlds then support learner-adaptive task and environment augmentation within source-supported behavior. From 1,570 traces, Trace2World constructs 50 environments. On 200 workflows across ten apps, 91.1% are reproduced end to end, versus 59.8% for the strongest matched task-local baseline. Source-grounded validation retains 94.0% of simulated training gains on real devices, versus 54.7% under self-validation. Learner guidance raises benchmark success from 56.9% to 61.1%. Training in Trace2World further improves the model by 20.2 points on our benchmark, 5.4--16.2 points across four external GUI benchmarks, and 16.3 points on 100 real-device tasks. Reliable reconstruction separates what behavior source evidence supports from whether the implementation preserves it.

Machine Learning.title: Bridging the Data Gap: Source-Informed Task-Space Transport for Few-Shot Diffusion
Machine Learning.summary:
arXiv:2610.31323v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: When an object category is well represented in one domain but scarcely observed in another, adapting a diffusion model to the target can be unreliable. Yet the same source-target relationship may have been observed for other categories. We ask whether this recurring relation can be learned and reused for a new semantic task. We introduce Meta-Diff, which embeds source and target distributions in a shared low-dimensional task space, learns an affine transport map across paired training tasks, and generates from the transported source coordinate using a shared diffusion backbone. At deployment, it requires source examples and the identity of a previously learned relation, but neither target images nor target-specific optimisation. Gaussian-mixture experiments examine how transfer depends on task information retained by the encoder, relation predictability and the size of the source--target shift. On held-out CIFAR-100 validation tasks, correct-source transport achieves 13.9% lower mean sliced Wasserstein distance than wrong-source transport. In the one-target final-test comparison, it achieves 14.7% lower mean distance than target-only adaptation and 32.7% lower than full fine-tuning under validation-selected settings. These gains have clear limits: directly applying the known corruption to clean-source generations performs better on CIFAR, and requested-class identity remains weak. Office-Home shows domain alignment without reliable object identity; clinical stress tests show no resolved source-specific advantage. The results characterise when reusable task-space relations help and where their generative limitations remain.

Machine Learning.title: Reactive Optimizers
Machine Learning.summary:
arXiv:2610.33826v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: We study a reactive optimizer that uses a pretrained language-model agent to inspect training dynamics and rewrite executable optimizer code during a single training run. The agent can change update rules and schedules for individual parameter groups, without optimizer-specific meta-training or memory transferred from other runs. We evaluate this approach, OPAL, on language modeling and image generation when a recipe has not been tuned for the target setting. Across the evaluated settings, it matches or improves on selected fixed recipes. Analysis of its decisions shows changes to learning-rate schedules, optimizer structure, numerical precision, and momentum. Controlled experiments also show adaptation to repeated data corruption and reduced overfitting. We report these behaviors together with the agent's computational cost and implementation requirements.

Machine Learning.title: Last-Iterate Stationarity of Muon with Finitely Many Newton-Schulz Iterations
Machine Learning.summary:
arXiv:2610.34158v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Muon has demonstrated strong empirical performance in large-scale language-model training, motivating a deeper theoretical understanding of its practical implementation. Unlike the idealized polar-factor update, practical Muon employs a fixed number of quintic Newton-Schulz iterations. Existing analyses primarily establish average- or best-iterate stationarity guarantees, while last-iterate convergence remains less understood. In this work, we investigate last-iterate gradient convergence of practical finite-step Muon on smooth, lower-bounded nonconvex objectives. In the deterministic setting, we show that Muon without input stabilization can exhibit cyclic behavior even on a smooth convex quadratic. In contrast, with positive stabilization, we establish last-iterate gradient convergence and square-summability of gradients for any fixed momentum coefficient below one and a sufficiently small constant learning rate. In the stochastic setting, we first demonstrate that persistent bounded, unbiased noise can prevent convergence under fixed learning rates and momentum, even with positive stabilization. We then establish almost-sure and mean-square last-iterate gradient convergence under bounded-variance stochastic gradients by combining diminishing learning rates with increasing momentum. Finally, we construct a smooth counterexample demonstrating that neither convergence theorem implies a pointwise polynomial convergence rate. Nevertheless, we establish density-one convergence rates, guaranteeing polynomial gradient decay for all but an asymptotically vanishing fraction of iterations.

Machine Learning.title: A Hybrid Framework for Explainable Aviation Risk: Causal Chain Extraction from Safety Reports with Physics-Based Failure Quantification and Interventional Analysis
Machine Learning.summary:
arXiv:2610.35658v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Aviation authorities hold decades of accident reports whose narratives record how investigators reconstructed each accident. Computational work on these archives has mostly sorted reports into fixed taxonomies. In this work, we propose a hybrid framework in which a text-based corpus identifies the leading factors of a failure mode. Physics-based models then quantify how likely that failure is at a stated operating point. Ordered causal chains extracted from 56{,}202 American accident reports with a local large language model aggregate into a causation knowledge graph. On an evaluation sample of 2{,}000 reports, the chains recover 90.8\% of investigator-flagged causes. Each physical factor whose drivers the record carries receives an occurrence model calibrated to the accident population. A leaky noisy-OR fitted to the corpus combines the factors into a failure mode probability that supports intervention. For engine power loss, the carburetor icing model separates 1{,}205 icing accidents from other accidents using temperature and dewpoint alone, reaching 0.61 in area under the receiver operating characteristic curve against a density ratio ceiling of 0.64. Routine weather hours give no valid control, because flying concentrates in fair weather. On later years the physics adds 0.03 to that area for occurrence and nothing for severity, so its value lies in interpretability. On four named accidents, abduction gives a probability of necessity of 0.29 to 0.50 for the heat omission, under monotonicity. The Fast Causal Inference algorithm does not license the largest backdoor adjustment on the learned networks.

Machine Learning.title: Communication-Efficient Clustered Federated Learning in Non-IID Wireless Networks
Machine Learning.summary:
arXiv:2610.38970v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Current and emerging mobile networks face increasing privacy, scalability, and performance challenges as distributed learning becomes essential for advanced 6G services. These challenges are amplified by the presence of non-IID data, naturally arising in heterogeneous wireless environments, that degrade the performance of standard Federated Learning (FL) approaches. To address non-IID data across clients, we propose a Clustered Federated Learning (CFL) framework that assigns clients to specialized models during training. Data-domain clustering initializes model-based clustering, enabling identification and exploitation of client similarities without sharing raw data while reducing communication cost.
  Motivated by mmWave beam selection, we evaluate our methods on a wireless simulation dataset (DeepMIMO) and complement it with two non-IID benchmarks (FEMNIST, Rotated CIFAR-10) to isolate different non-IID characteristics. Our best configurations improve accuracy over IFCA by 4.8 pp on DeepMIMO and 10.6 pp on FEMNIST while reducing downlink data volume by 83.1 % on FEMNIST compared to IFCA.
  We demonstrate that different clustering strategies suit different non-IID characteristics. These results show that our CFL methods enable resource-efficient, and high-performance distributed learning in future 6G networks.

Machine Learning.title: TensorSSM: Memorizing Spatial Position in Dynamic State Space for Tensor Core Generation
Machine Learning.summary:
arXiv:2610.40871v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: High-dimensional tensors are ubiquitous in real-world applications but lead to massive storage overhead. Functional tensor decomposition addresses this by employing neural networks to map element coordinates to tensor cores, significantly reducing the parameters for data compression. However, existing functional methods typically flatten high-order tensors into 1D sequences. This folding operation causes highly overlapping local coordinate sequences and struggles to capture complex cross-mode spatial dependencies, severely limiting their expressiveness on diverse datasets. To tackle these challenges, we propose TensorSSM, a novel Implicit Neural Representation (INR) for functional decomposition method that memorizes spatial positions within a dynamic State Space Model (SSM). Specifically, TensorSSM first decomposes mode-wise coordinates into sequences spit by K-ary rule, encoding spatial tokens from coarse to fine, which effectively captures spatial variations. Furthermore, we extend the SSM's state space to explicitly map cross-mode spatial dependencies, allowing inter-mode interactions to enhance the updates of each mode. By integrating cross-mode information from previous hidden states into the current state transitions, TensorSSM effectively expands tensor representation along two dimensions: the sequence dimension for coarse-to-fine spatial tokens, and the state dimension for cross-mode memorization. This design effectively integrates spatial information into the state space and the tensor core, substantially advancing the state adaptability and enhancing the expressiveness of the data compression. Extensive experiments demonstrate that TensorSSM achieves significantly high reconstruction accuracy and storage efficiency, exhibiting robust expressiveness across diverse tensor datasets without relying on strict spatial assumptions.

Machine Learning.title: Wave Physics as Representation: Tensor-Structured Neural Reconstruction for Ocean Acoustic Fields
Machine Learning.summary:
arXiv:2611.01680v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Reconstructing three-dimensional (3D) complex ocean acoustic fields from sparse measurements is challenging due to highly oscillatory wave structures and restricted sensing patterns/routes. Learning-based approaches fall into two categories. First, purely data-driven models can learn complex field patterns, but do not explicitly exploit wave physics that may enhance interpretability and reduce training costs. Second, physics-informed methods impose a specified physical equation as a reconstruction constraint, but often require environment-dependent parameters that are difficult to acquire. As a result, practical 3D acoustic field reconstruction that is both physically grounded and robust to uncertain environmental information remains largely unexplored. This work takes an alternative route: instead of solving a fully specified wave equation, it extracts a structured representation from wave physics and learns its components from data. From the Helmholtz equation and normal mode propagation, we derive a structured spatial-angular tensor representation, termed the S/c representation. Under a low-rank specialization, it takes the form of a rank-(L,L,1) block-term tensor decomposition, which connects structured sampling patterns/routes used in ocean sensing to sufficient conditions for field recovery. Building on this tensor representation, we propose TIDAL, a neural reconstructor that uses the S/c representation as an inductive bias for structured decoding and aligns information aggregation with the sampling geometry. The neural learner removes the need for known model parameters required by conventional physics-based recovery methods. Experiments across three structured sampling geometries show that TIDAL achieves the best reconstruction performance and fastest inference among baselines, with benefits from the physics-derived representation under limited data and model capacity.

Machine Learning.title: NorthCUA Technical Report: Turbocharging Computer-Use Agents through Experience at Scale
Machine Learning.summary:
arXiv:2611.02102v3 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Scaling computer-use agents from individual actions to complex software work requires experience that connects decisions to complete outcomes. We present NorthCUA, an integrated system for turbocharging computer-use agents through experience at scale. Its Experience Flywheel supplies diverse executable tasks to the NorthCUA Harness, which sustains long interactions, records decisions, and checks task outcomes. The Flywheel uses these records to curate verified trajectories. For unsolved tasks, recursive self-improvement evolves reusable skills and preserves verified milestones so later attempts build on earlier progress. Staged Learning combines this experience with grounding data from the Flywheel to develop GUI competence through mid-training and long-horizon supervised fine-tuning. The policy then learns from fresh attempts in the same Harness through joint desktop-web reinforcement learning, closing the loop between experience production and policy improvement. The resulting Nano, Mini, and Pro family achieves state-of-the-art results among open-source models across GUI grounding, desktop execution, and Web interaction under the reported evaluation settings. For more responsive Web workflows, NorthCUA-Ultrafast pairs direct action selection with open-ended generation on pre-RL Nano, offering a measured quality-latency tradeoff. Together, these advances establish NorthCUA as a high-performing model family and a reusable foundation for agents that carry complex software work from intent to completion.

Machine Learning.title: Restrained Diffusion Bridges: Targeted Denoiser Training and Refinement
Machine Learning.summary:
arXiv:2611.02170v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Diffusion models are often inaccurate in critical, data-sparse regions of the target distribution. Sampling from restrained distributions, biased distributions used in classical enhanced sampling to concentrate data near chosen configurations, can control where training data are collected but biases the learned distribution. We establish that this bias cancels exactly when forward noising from restrained data is conditioned on the restrained configuration at an appropriately chosen intermediate time. This allows a pretrained model fine-tuned on restrained data to achieve high accuracy in any chosen region of the target distribution, regardless of its probability, using standard denoising or flow matching objectives without importance weights. When no target data are available, Gibbs sampling enables inference from a model trained exclusively on restrained data.

Machine Learning.title: Thought-deciphering via hierarchical EEG-to-text alignment
Machine Learning.summary:
arXiv:2611.03623v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Non-invasive brain-to-text interfaces offer alternative communication pathways for people with communication disabilities. However, sentence-level decoding from electroencephalography (EEG) remains challenging. We propose a hierarchical EEG-text alignment framework that retrieves sentences by progressively decoding coarse-grained semantic information and fine-grained sentence representations. We hypothesize that broader semantic context can be more reliably captured from EEG than individual sentences. Accordingly, EEG representations are first aligned with semantic classes, followed by sentence retrieval within the predicted class. Among over 2,000 unique text samples, our approach achieves average top-5 and top-10 retrieval accuracies of 62.6\% $\pm$ 1.0\% and 83.5\% $\pm$ 1.0\%, respectively, compared with 50.3\% $\pm$ 2.3\% and 68.3\% $\pm$ 2.0\% for direct EEG-sentence alignment. Qualitative analysis further reveals that decoding performance depends strongly on textual context. These findings demonstrate the potential of hierarchical semantic alignment for improving sentence-level EEG-to-text decoding.

Machine Learning.title: Pretraining Data Scale Reverses the Muon-AdamW Fine-Tuning Gap
Machine Learning.summary:
arXiv:2611.03633v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Muon has recently emerged as a promising optimizer for pretraining large language models, offering a speedup over AdamW in minimizing pretraining loss. However, it remains unclear whether Muon's advantage persists after fine-tuning. In this paper, we study the downstream behavior of Muon and AdamW and uncover a surprising trend: beyond a sufficiently large pretraining data budget, AdamW outperforms Muon after fine-tuning. Moreover, as model size increases, AdamW overtakes Muon at progressively smaller pretraining token-parameter ratios. To explain this reversal, we view fine-tuning as a perturbation of the outputs and introduce the margin-to-spread ratio, which measures how far the correct logit lies above the wrong ones relative to how widely the wrong logits are spread. In language models, Muon has the larger margin-to-spread ratio at small data budgets and AdamW at large ones, mirroring the fine-tuning trend. In a linear associative memory, we prove that after one update the margin-to-spread ratio of gradient descent gains on that of Muon as the data budget grows, and simulations show that this trend persists after extended training.

Machine Learning.title: Separating Common and Unique Directions for Model Merging
Machine Learning.summary:
arXiv:2611.04108v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Model merging combines multiple fine-tuned models without additional training, and arithmetic methods have emerged as a simple yet effective way to merge models without data. However, existing arithmetic methods treat task vectors in parameter space and apply a single element-wise rule to directions that can differ in mergeability. In a shared directional basis, we find a consistent two-regime structure: a low-dispersion common bulk shared across tasks and a high-dispersion task-dominated tail that carries disproportionate energy. These findings motivate Common--Unique Subspace Decomposition (CUSD), a data-free pre-merging method that separates task vectors into common and unique directional components, merges the common components with a downstream arithmetic operator, and retains unique residuals separately. Experiments across $11$ base models, four model families, and four arithmetic-based merging operators show that CUSD improves 42 of 44 model--operator combinations and achieves up to 22.5% improvement over the corresponding baselines. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/stwang666/CUSD
Machine Learning.comment: Comments: Accepted by NeurIPS 2026

Machine Learning.title: Aligning Training and Rollout Policies for End-to-End FP4 RL on Mixture-of-Experts LLMs
Machine Learning.summary:
arXiv:2611.04376v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: In this work, we study end-to-end FP4 reinforcement learning (RL) post-training for Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) large language models. Recent work on FP4 RL has introduced effective recovery recipes that restore accuracy under aggressive low-precision quantization for dense models, but we find that the same approach yields no improvement over the naive FP4 baseline in the MoE setting. We conduct an in-depth study to understand why. Our analysis identifies the root cause in the routing mechanism unique to MoE: because the router makes discrete expert-selection decisions, training-inference policy alignment becomes acutely sensitive to whether the same recovery technique is applied symmetrically on the training and inference sides. When an asymmetric recipe is used-including the dense-model approach, which corrects only the rollout-training-inference alignment deteriorates sharply, as measured by the Pearson correlation coefficient between training and inference probabilities, and router selection matching rates. Building on this finding, we propose MoEResQ, a quantization-recovery recipe for MoE RL post-training that enforces symmetry between the training- and inference-side corrections. MoEResQ restores training-inference alignment and substantially closes the accuracy gap to full precision, establishing symmetric recovery as the key principle in FP4 RL for MoE models.

Machine Learning.title: Sample-Grained Approximate Unlearning with Provable Per-Sample Bounds
Machine Learning.summary:
arXiv:2611.04501v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Machine unlearning aims to erase the influence of a designated forget set from a trained model while preserving strong utility on the retain set. Approximate unlearning methods efficiently achieve this goal without full retraining, but their effectiveness is primarily assessed using dataset-level aggregate metrics. These aggregate metrics can mask deviations from retraining at the level of individual samples. In this work, we focus on per-sample unlearning effectiveness. We introduce SALA (Sample-grained Likelihoods ALignment), a plug-in optimization framework that enables approximate unlearning methods to operate at the level of individual samples by steering each example toward its correct target distribution. To quantitatively assess this behavior, we further propose the sample-grained distribution gap, a metric that captures per-sample discrepancies between approximate unlearning and exact retraining output distributions. We provide theoretical guarantees showing that SALA contracts this gap and yields a bounded per-sample discrepancy to retraining. To make this framework practical, we develop a low-cost estimation method for the member and non-member target distributions. Extensive experiments on classification and generation tasks demonstrate that SALA reduces the sample-grained distribution gap by up to $86.67\%$ when paired with existing approximate unlearning baselines, while also improving robustness to unlearning hyperparameters.
Machine Learning.comment: Comments: accepted by NeurIPS 2026

Machine Learning.title: FedCSGA: Evolutionary Client Selection with Joint Statistical and System Heterogeneity in Federated Learning
Machine Learning.summary:
arXiv:2611.04667v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Federated Learning (FL) enables collaborative training of machine learning models across distributed clients while preserving data privacy. In practical deployments, FL relies on selecting a client subset in each communication round to reduce communication cost, mitigate stragglers, and improve training efficiency under heterogeneous data and system conditions. In heterogeneous edge computing environments, both statistical heterogeneity and system heterogeneity significantly affect convergence efficiency and model performance. However, existing client selection methods often address these factors independently, overlooking their coupled and dynamic impact across communication rounds. To address this limitation, we propose FedCSGA, a Client Selection method for Federated learning based on Genetic Algorithm. FedCSGA encodes client subsets as chromosomes and evaluates these subsets through a non-linear fitness function that jointly integrates resource-aware metrics and history-aware participation weighting. This design captures subset-level interactions, mitigates persistent selection bias, and balances statistical utility with system efficiency. Extensive experiments on FMNIST, CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and Tiny-ImageNet demonstrate that FedCSGA consistently outperforms state-of-the-art baselines across diverse heterogeneity settings, achieving accuracy improvements of up to 7.0% and faster convergence with fewer communication rounds. These results validate the effectiveness of jointly modeling statistical and system factors to achieve robust and efficient learning in heterogeneous federated environments.

Machine Learning.title: PAC Learning with Multiple Correct Answers
Machine Learning.summary:
arXiv:2611.05133v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: We study PAC learning when each example comes with a set of at most $\ell$ correct labels and a prediction is correct if it belongs to this set. Training may reveal the full set, only whether a proposed label is correct (bandit feedback), or one correct label chosen by a demonstrator (demonstrations). Our main finding is that demonstrations can be much harder than full sets, and even than bandit feedback, both in which classes can be learned and in how many examples are needed. For finite label spaces, a generalized Natarajan dimension characterizes learnability from full sets and from bandit feedback, in both the realizable and the agnostic setting. From demonstrations, however, a class is realizably learnable if and only if the intersections of at most $\ell+1$ of its hypotheses are learnable from full sets. Already with three labels, this condition can fail for a class learnable from a single full-set example or even a single bandit answer. When the condition holds, we show that $\widetilde O(\varepsilon^{-\ell})$ demonstrations suffice, and the exponent $\ell$ cannot be improved in general, even for classes learnable from $\widetilde O(1/\varepsilon)$ full sets or bandit answers. For countable label spaces and $\ell \geq 2$, our packed dimension, which asks for many disjoint groups of at most $\ell+1$ hypotheses with no common label, characterizes full-set learnability, and demonstrations still reduce to intersections. Agnostic learning from demonstrations, already for finite label spaces, is not determined by the dimensions of the intersection class that characterize realizable learning. Finally, we show that the uniform bound $\ell$ on the number of correct labels is essential. Without this bound, it is impossible to characterize learnability by any dimension determined by finite subclasses.

Machine Learning.title: Stabilizing On-Policy Targeted Guidance in Agentic Reinforcement Learning
Machine Learning.summary:
arXiv:2611.05266v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Naive on-policy RL is often bottlenecked by the capabilities of the base model --- insufficient coverage can result in an inability to learn from certain rewards. At the same time, rewards in modern post-training systems often come from rich textual sources, e.g. judge models with a rubric of criteria. Can we utilize such structures to provide a rich directional signal that enables improving on otherwise difficult to optimize rewards? In this work, we examine a framework we refer to as targeted guidance that learns from per-turn textual feedback via an on-policy self-distillation objective. Our focus is not only on directly improving hard-to-optimize behaviors, but on how to do so throughout the training process without degrading baseline RL performance. Over a range of settings across an agentic multi-turn software engineering environment, we find success by combining targeted self-distillation with a per-criteria RL reward, and by limiting feedback to turns where the policy specifically fails. We further examine the design choices that lead to stable entropy and reduce oscillatory behavior throughout training.

Machine Learning.title: Exploring Sequence Feature Alignment for Domain Adaptive Detection Transformers
Machine Learning.summary:
arXiv:2107.12636v5 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Detection transformers have recently shown promising object detection results and attracted increasing attention. However, how to develop effective domain adaptation techniques to improve its cross-domain performance remains unexplored and unclear. In this paper, we delve into this topic and empirically find that direct feature distribution alignment on the CNN backbone only brings limited improvements, as it does not guarantee domain-invariant sequence features in the transformer for prediction. To address this issue, we propose a novel Sequence Feature Alignment (SFA) method that is specially designed for the adaptation of detection transformers. Technically, SFA consists of a domain query-based feature alignment (DQFA) module and a token-wise feature alignment (TDA) module. In DQFA, a novel domain query is used to aggregate and align global context from the token sequence of both domains. DQFA reduces the domain discrepancy in global feature representations and object relations when deploying in the transformer encoder and decoder, respectively. Meanwhile, TDA aligns token features in the sequence from both domains, which reduces the domain gaps in local and instance-level feature representations in the transformer encoder and decoder, respectively. Besides, a novel bipartite matching consistency loss is proposed to enhance the feature discriminability for robust object detection. Experiments on three challenging benchmarks show that SFA outperforms state-of-the-art domain adaptive object detection methods. Code has been made available at: https://github.com/encounter1997/SFA.

Machine Learning.title: Questioning Representational Optimism in Deep Learning: The Fractured Entangled Representation Hypothesis
Machine Learning.summary:
arXiv:2505.11581v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Much of the excitement in modern AI is driven by the observation that scaling up existing systems leads to better performance. But does better performance necessarily imply better internal representations? While the representational optimist assumes it must, this position paper challenges that view. We compare neural networks evolved through an open-ended search process to networks trained via conventional stochastic gradient descent (SGD) on the simple task of generating a single image. This minimal setup offers a unique advantage: each hidden neuron's full functional behavior can be easily visualized as an image, thus revealing how the network's output behavior is internally constructed neuron by neuron. The result is striking: while both networks produce the same output behavior, their internal representations differ dramatically. The SGD-trained networks exhibit a form of disorganization that we term fractured entangled representation (FER). Interestingly, the evolved networks largely lack FER, even approaching a unified factored representation (UFR). In large models, FER may be degrading core model capacities like generalization, creativity, and (continual) learning. Therefore, understanding and mitigating FER could be critical to the future of representation learning.

Machine Learning.title: When Reviews Are Scarce: Structure-Aware Review Imputation for Recommendation in Realistic Sparse Review Settings
Machine Learning.summary:
arXiv:2508.01128v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Textual reviews enrich recommender systems with fine-grained preference signals and enhanced explainability. However, in real-world scenarios, users rarely leave reviews, resulting in severe sparsity that undermines the effectiveness of review-aware recommenders under partial observability. A natural remedy is to synthesize the missing reviews to restore the textual signal these recommenders rely on. Yet, conventional imputation techniques, such as matrix completion and LLM-based augmentation, either lose contextualized semantics by embedding texts into vectors or overlook structural dependencies on the user-item graph. To address these shortcomings, we propose TWISTER (ToWards Imputation on Sparsity with Textual Edge Graph Representation), a unified framework for sparse-text recommendation that synthesizes missing reviews by jointly modeling semantic and structural signals. Specifically, we represent user-item interactions as a Textual-Edge Graph (TEG), treating reviews as edge attributes. To capture relational context, we construct line-graph views and employ an LLM as a graph-aware aggregator. For each interaction lacking a textual review, our model aggregates natural-language representations from neighboring interactions to generate a coherent and personalized review. Experiments on multiple datasets show that TWISTER consistently outperforms traditional numeric, graph-based, and LLM baselines, delivering higher-quality imputed reviews and, more importantly, improved downstream recommendation. In summary, TWISTER is a drop-in, structure-aware imputer that recovers the textual signal that review-aware recommenders need when reviews are scarce.

Machine Learning.title: Population-Aligned Persona Generation for LLM-based Social Simulation
Machine Learning.summary:
arXiv:2509.10127v3 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Recent advances in large language models (LLMs) have enabled large-scale, high-fidelity social simulations, creating new opportunities for computational social science. However, constructing persona sets that faithfully reflect real-world population diversity remains a key challenge. Existing studies often emphasize agentic frameworks and simulation environments, while paying less attention to persona generation and the biases introduced by unrepresentative persona sets. In this paper, we propose a systematic framework for synthesizing high-quality, population-aligned persona sets for LLM-driven social simulation. Our approach begins by leveraging LLMs to generate narrative personas from long-term social media data, followed by rigorous quality assessment to filter out low-fidelity profiles. We then apply importance sampling to achieve global alignment with reference psychometric distributions, such as the Big Five personality traits. To address the needs of specific simulation contexts, we further introduce a task-specific module that adapts the globally aligned persona set to targeted subpopulations. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our method significantly reduces population-level bias and enables accurate, flexible social simulation for a wide range of research and policy applications.

Machine Learning.title: UpSafe$^\circ$C: Upcycling for Controllable Safety in Large Language Models
Machine Learning.summary:
arXiv:2510.02194v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have achieved remarkable progress across a wide range of tasks, but remain vulnerable to safety risks such as harmful content generation and jailbreak attacks. Existing safety techniques---including external guardrails, inference-time guidance, and post-training alignment---each face limitations in balancing safety, utility, and controllability. In this work, we propose UpSafe$^\circ$C, a unified framework for enhancing LLM safety through safety-aware upcycling. Our approach first identifies safety-critical layers and upcycles them into a sparse Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) structure, where the router acts as a soft guardrail that selectively activates original MLPs and added safety experts. We further introduce a two-stage SFT strategy to strengthen safety discrimination while preserving general capabilities. To enable flexible control at inference time, we introduce a safety temperature mechanism, allowing dynamic adjustment of the trade-off between safety and utility. Experiments across multiple benchmarks, base model, and model scales demonstrate that UpSafe$^\circ$C achieves robust safety improvements against harmful and jailbreak inputs, while maintaining competitive performance on general tasks. Moreover, analysis shows that safety temperature provides fine-grained inference-time control that achieves controllable trade-off between utility and safety. Our results highlight a new direction for LLM safety: moving from static alignment toward dynamic, modular, and inference-aware control. Code: https://github.com/HansSunY/UpSafe.

Machine Learning.title: Bilevel Learning via Strategically Inexact Stochastic Gradient Descent
Machine Learning.summary:
arXiv:2511.06774v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Bilevel optimization is a central tool in computational imaging for high-dimensional hyperparameter tuning; prominent applications include learning data-adaptive regularizers and optimizing forward operators in variational regularization. However, due to the nested nature of the problem, exact gradients with respect to the parameters (so-called hypergradients) are not available: the precision of the hypergradient is linearly related to the computational cost, thus requiring algorithms which can solve the problem without unnecessary precision. In learned-regularizer pipelines, the inner reconstruction solver is typically run for a fixed number of iterations, leaving the hypergradient accuracy uncontrolled and existing convergence theory inapplicable. In this work, we analyze the schedules that practitioners actually run: we prove convergence of inexact stochastic bilevel optimization and establish rates under both decaying accuracy and step size schedules, showing that, with optimal configurations, convergence occurs at an $O(k^{-1/4})$ rate in expectation. This is the optimal rate of nonconvex stochastic gradient descent and matches single-loop stochastic bilevel methods; with warm-started inner solves, total costs also agree up to constants. Experiments on image denoising and inpainting with convex ridge regularizers and input-convex neural networks confirm our analysis: decreasing step sizes improve stability, accuracy scheduling is more critical than step size strategy, and adaptive preconditioning (e.g., Adam) further boosts performance, particularly for input-convex neural networks. In a budget-matched comparison with four state-of-the-art single-loop methods, accuracy-scheduled stochastic gradient descent and its Adam variant attain the highest test peak signal-to-noise ratio.

Machine Learning.title: Online learning of subgrid-scale models for quasi-geostrophic turbulence in planetary interiors
Machine Learning.summary:
arXiv:2511.14581v3 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Machine learning approaches to subgrid-scale (SGS) modeling are now well established in atmospheric and oceanic applications. Among these, online end-to-end learning, where the differentiable solver participates in the training, has shown particular promise. Yet existing studies are largely restricted to idealised periodic domains, with no mechanical boundaries, precluding them from addressing the dynamics of bounded rotating flows relevant to planetary interiors. Here we consider two-dimensional quasi-geostrophic turbulence in a rapidly rotating annular bounded domain. We examine three configurations varying the geometry of the container and the rotation rate. The system exhibits key features such as zonal jets, Rossby waves, and, in the spherical shell geometry, a slow quasi-periodic inward drift of the jets. The spectral properties of the zonal and non-zonal flow can be understood in the framework of zonostrophic turbulence theory. We develop a differentiable solver for this system, which allows us to train SGS models online, over a time span of one turnover time, using coarse-grained data from direct numerical simulations. In all cases, a SGS model trained on a single turnover time accurately reproduces global integrated diagnostics, energy spectra as well as long-term dynamical behaviours, such as jet migration, occurring on timescales which exceed the training window by one order of magnitude. The online-trained model further outperforms classical hyperdiffusivity and Leith closure schemes, for which reducing the radial resolution is impractical. The resulting speed-up paves the way to further investigations of long-term geophysical fluid processes beyond the reach of direct numerical simulations.

Machine Learning.title: From Lab to Reality: A Practical Evaluation of Deep Learning Models and LLMs for Vulnerability Detection
Machine Learning.summary:
arXiv:2512.10485v4 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Vulnerability detection methods based on deep learning (DL) have shown strong performance on benchmark datasets, yet their real-world effectiveness remains underexplored. Recent work suggests that graph neural network-based and transformer-based models, including large language models (LLMs), yield promising results when evaluated on curated benchmark datasets. These datasets are typically characterized by similar data distributions and may contain synthetic samples, heuristic labels, or labeling noise. In this study, we systematically evaluate four representative DL models---Devign, ReVeal, LineVul, and VulBERTa---across four representative datasets: Juliet, Devign, BigVul, and ICVul. Each model is trained independently on each dataset, and the graph-based and CodeBERT representations adopted by these models are analyzed using t-SNE and centroid distance to examine vulnerability-related patterns. To assess realistic applicability, we further evaluate trained ReVeal and LineVul models, along with four open-weight LLMs, on VentiVul, our newly constructed temporally separated out-of-distribution (OOD) dataset comprising 200 recent vulnerabilities from Linux and Chromium. Our experiments reveal that current representation methods struggle to distinguish vulnerable from non-vulnerable code and that trained models generalize poorly across datasets with differing distributions and characteristics. When evaluated on VentiVul, performance drops sharply, with most models failing to detect vulnerabilities reliably or distinguish vulnerable functions from their patched counterparts. These results expose a persistent gap between academic benchmarks and real-world deployment, emphasizing the value of our deployment-oriented evaluation framework and the need for more robust code representations, higher-quality datasets, and evaluation methods that account for vulnerability-fixing changes.

Machine Learning.title: Deep Sets and event-level maximum-likelihood estimation for fast pile-up jet rejection at the ATLAS High Level Trigger
Machine Learning.summary:
arXiv:2512.10819v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Multiple proton-proton interactions occur in the same bunch crossing at the LHC ("pile-up"), with the mean number of interactions per bunch crossing reaching up to about 60 in Run 3 and up to about 200 at the High-Luminosity LHC. As a direct consequence, hadronic activity within each bunch crossing increases, making it more difficult to identify collisions of interest pertaining to multijet final states. This work introduces DIPz, an uncertainty-aware Deep Sets-based machine-learning model that estimates each jet's origin along the beam axis as a Gaussian likelihood using the set of charged-particle tracks matched to the jet. Next, the DIPz predictions for each jet are combined into a likelihood-based event-level discriminant, which is optimised to select events compatible with a single collision producing a given jet multiplicity. This combined approach provides a robust and computationally efficient method for pile-up rejection in multijet final states, applicable to real-time event selections at the ATLAS High Level Trigger (HLT). Deployed online during Run 3 data taking, this approach reduces background rates by more than a factor of two, and decreases CPU consumption by approximately one third relative to the baseline data-taking configuration. It provides an early, flavour-agnostic pile-up jet rejection layer at the HLT preselection stage, introducing a previously unavailable handle for high-multiplicity jet signatures targeted by ATLAS.

Machine Learning.title: Optimality-Informed Neural Networks for Solving Parametric Optimization Problems
Machine Learning.summary:
arXiv:2512.20270v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Many engineering tasks require solving families of nonlinear constrained optimization problems, parametrized in setting-specific variables. This is computationally demanding, particularly if solutions have to be computed across strongly varying parameter values, e.g., in real-time control or for model-based design. Thus, we propose to learn the mapping from parameters to the primal optimal solutions and to their corresponding duals using neural networks, giving a dense estimation in contrast to gridded approaches. Our approach, Optimality-Informed Neural Networks (OptINNs), combines (i) a KKT-residual loss that penalizes violations of the first-order optimality conditions under standard constraint qualification assumptions, and (ii) problem-specific output activations that enforce simple inequality constraints (e.g., box-type/positivity) by construction. This design reduces data requirements, allows the prediction of dual variables, and improves feasibility and closeness to optimality compared to penalty-only training. Taking quadratic penalties as a baseline, as previously proposed for this problem class in the literature, our method simplifies hyperparameter tuning and attains tighter adherence to optimality conditions. We evaluate OptINNs on different nonlinear optimization problems ranging from low to high dimensions and compare them with equally sized neural networks trained using the quadratic-penalty method. On small problems, OptINNs match a quadratic-penalty baseline in primal accuracy while additionally predicting dual variables with low error. On larger problems, OptINNs achieve lower constraint violations, lower primal error, and lower errors in the predicted costs. These results suggest that embedding feasibility and optimality into the network architecture and loss can make learning-based surrogates more accurate, feasible, and data-efficient for parametric optimization.

Machine Learning.title: Stabilizing Off-policy LLM Optimization with Prefix Importance Ratio
Machine Learning.summary:
arXiv:2601.22718v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) post-training has increasingly demonstrated strong ability to elicit reasoning behaviors in large language models (LLMs). For training efficiency, rollouts are typically generated in an off-policy manner using an older sampling policy and then used to update the current target policy. To correct the resulting discrepancy between the sampling and target policies, most existing RL objectives rely on a token-level importance sampling ratio. However, we observe unstable training dynamics in existing importance-weighted objectives under large policy lag. In this paper, we revisit LLM policy optimization under off-policy conditions and show that the exact correction for the prefix-marginal policy gradient is the cumulative prefix importance ratio. Token-level weighting does not explicitly correct for this prefix distribution shift. To stabilize LLM optimization under large off-policy drift, we propose a simple yet effective objective, Minimum Prefix Ratio (MinPRO). MinPRO replaces the unstable cumulative prefix ratio with a biased, non-cumulative surrogate based on the minimum token-level ratio observed in the preceding prefix. Extensive experiments on both dense and mixture-of-experts LLMs, across multiple mathematical reasoning benchmarks, demonstrate that MinPRO substantially improves training stability and peak performance in off-policy regimes.

Machine Learning.title: From Outcome to Representation: Tracing Reasoning Mechanisms through Integrated Policy Gradient
Machine Learning.summary:
arXiv:2602.02313v3 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) demonstrate remarkable reasoning capabilities, yet the internal mechanisms driving these multi-step processes remain opaque. Existing mechanistic interpretability approaches often rely on superficial text-pattern co-occurrences or capture only short-term effects, struggling to trace the long-horizon, outcome-driven influence of internal components such as neurons or sparse features in multi-step reasoning.In this paper, we introduce Integrated Policy Gradient (IPG), a novel, training-free framework that brings policy-based attribution into mechanistic interpretability for LLM reasoning. Grounded in \textit{outcome-oriented} and \textit{sequential-influence-aware} principles, it backpropagates outcome-level, non-differentiable behavioral signals (e.g., reasoning outcome correctness) through entire inference trajectories, utilizing path integration to isolate outcome-relevant mediators at component level for reliable attribution. This provides a linear approximation of Causal Mediation Analysis (CMA) in reasoning. Empirical evaluations demonstrate that \method achieves precise localization and reveals mechanistic insights by identifying sparse, concentrated subsets of internal components associated with specific reasoning behaviors. Our method also enables modulation of reasoning capabilities, offering a powerful and reliable framework for understanding LLM reasoning. The project page is at https://foundation-model-research.github.io/IPG .

Machine Learning.title: Discovering Semantic Structures in Psychological Scales: A Response-Free Front-End to Efficient Simplification
Machine Learning.summary:
arXiv:2602.12575v3 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Psychological scale refinement traditionally relies on response-based methods such as factor analysis, item response theory, and network psychometrics to uncover latent constructs and optimize item composition. Although rigorous, these approaches require large samples and may be constrained by data availability and cross-cultural comparability. Recent advances in natural language processing suggest that the wording of scale items contains construct-relevant semantic organization, offering a complementary response-free perspective. We introduce a topic-modeling framework that operationalizes item-level semantic structure for systematic scale simplification. Items are encoded using contextual sentence embeddings and grouped through density-based clustering to identify semantic topics without predefining their number. Within each cluster, class-based term weighting identifies representative keywords that summarize each topic and support an interpretable semantic pre-structure of the item pool. Semantically related clusters are hierarchically merged, and representative items are selected using structure-aware membership criteria within an integrated reduction pipeline. We evaluated the framework on three widely used instruments: DASS, IPIP, and EPOCH, covering negative affect, personality traits, and well-being. Results showed that the identified semantic topics often formed factor-like groupings aligned with established constructs. Representative items selected through semantic membership probabilities reduced item counts by 60.5% on average while maintaining acceptable psychometric properties and preserving factor correlation patterns. Our framework formalizes semantic topic structure as an inspectable front-end for scale construction and simplification. To facilitate adoption, we provide a visualization-supported tool enabling one-click semantic analysis and structured simplification.

Machine Learning.title: Evolutionary System Prompt Learning for Reinforcement Learning in LLMs
Machine Learning.summary:
arXiv:2602.14697v4 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Building agentic systems that can autonomously self-improve from experience is a longstanding goal of AI. Large language models (LLMs) today primarily self-improve via two mechanisms: self-reflection for context updates, and reinforcement learning (RL) for weight updates. In this work, we propose Evolutionary System Prompt Learning (E-SPL), a method for jointly improving a model's experiential context and its weights. In each RL iteration, E-SPL samples trajectories under multiple system prompts in parallel, then uses them to jointly update the weights with RL and evolve the system prompts with self-reflection. E-SPL encourages a natural division between procedural knowledge in weights and interpretable declarative knowledge in system prompts. Most notably, in an easy-to-hard generalization setting (AIME $\rightarrow$ BeyondAIME), E-SPL improves RL success rate from 38.8% $\rightarrow$ 45.1%. E-SPL also improves RL on AIME 2025 (56.3% $\rightarrow$ 60.6%), HMMT 2025 (50.0% $\rightarrow$ 52.7%), and agentic search (44.2% $\rightarrow$ 48.6% on gpt-oss-120b). Across all settings, E-SPL outperforms both RL-only and evolution-only baselines, demonstrating that weight updates and context updates are deeply synergistic and can together yield gains in generalization that neither achieves alone. Code is available at https://github.com/LunjunZhang/E-SPL.

Machine Learning.title: Quantifying Error Propagation and Model Collapse in Diffusion Models
Machine Learning.summary:
arXiv:2602.16601v3 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Machine learning models are increasingly trained or fine-tuned on synthetic data. Recursively training on such data has been observed to significantly degrade performance in a wide range of tasks, often characterized by a progressive drift away from the target distribution. In this work, we theoretically analyze this phenomenon in the setting of score-based diffusion models. For a realistic pipeline where each training round uses a combination of synthetic data and fresh samples from the target distribution, we obtain upper and lower bounds on the accumulated divergence between the generated and target distributions. Notably, to the best of our knowledge, this is the first lower bound on the divergence between the learned and target distributions, even for standard diffusion models. Our results allow us to characterize different regimes of drift, depending on the score estimation error and the proportion of fresh data used in each generation. In a certain regime, the accumulated divergence after several retraining rounds can be expressed as a discounted sum of score estimation errors made at each generation. We also provide empirical results on synthetic data and images to illustrate the theory.

Machine Learning.title: The minimal width of universal $p$-adic ReLU neural networks
Machine Learning.summary:
arXiv:2603.00064v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: We determine the minimal width of $p$-adic neural networks with the universal approximation property for continuous $\mathbb Q_p$-valued functions on compact open subsets with respect to the $L_q$ norms and the $C_1$ norm, where the activation function is a natural $p$-adic analogue of the ReLU function.

Machine Learning.title: Does Explanation Correctness Matter? Linking Computational XAI Evaluation to Human Understanding
Machine Learning.summary:
arXiv:2603.25251v3 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Explainable AI (XAI) methods are commonly evaluated using functional correctness metrics, also called faithfulness or fidelity, which estimate how closely an explanation reflects the model's reasoning. Higher correctness is assumed to produce better human understanding, but this link has not been tested with controlled levels. We conducted a user study (N=200) that manipulated explanation correctness at four levels (100%, 85%, 70%, 55%) in a synthetic time series classification task where participants could not rely on domain knowledge or visual intuition. Explanations were constructed to resemble feature attributions, with correctness defined against a known ground truth rather than estimated from a trained model. Participants predicted a simulated AI's decisions from these explanations (forward simulation), and we used their forward simulation accuracy as a proxy for understanding. Correctness affected forward simulation accuracy, but not at every level: accuracy dropped at 70% and 55% relative to 100%, with no further reduction below 70% and no conclusive difference between 85% and 100%. Lower correctness reduced how many participants predicted accurately rather than lowering accuracy uniformly, and even with fully correct explanations, only a subset of participants predicted well above chance. In exploratory analyses, some participants predicted decisions accurately but described the wrong pattern when asked what the AI used, and self-reported ratings correlated with forward simulation accuracy only when explanations were fully correct. These findings suggest that, for feature-attribution-style explanations, not all differences in functional correctness translate to differences in human understanding, highlighting the need to validate functional metrics against human outcomes.

Machine Learning.title: Quantum-Inspired Tensor Network Autoencoders for Anomaly Detection: A MERA-Based Approach
Machine Learning.summary:
arXiv:2604.06541v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: We investigate whether a multiscale tensor-network architecture provides a useful inductive bias for reconstruction-based anomaly detection in collider jets. Jets are produced by a branching cascade, so their internal structure is naturally organised across angular and momentum scales. This motivates an autoencoder that compresses information hierarchically and can reorganise short-range correlations before coarse-graining. Guided by this picture, we formulate a Multiscale Entanglement Renormalization Ansatz (MERA)-inspired autoencoder acting on ordered jet constituents. To our knowledge, a MERA-inspired autoencoder has not previously been proposed, and this architecture has not been explored in collider anomaly detection. We compare this architecture to a dense autoencoder, the corresponding tree-tensor-network limit, and classical baselines within a background-only reconstruction framework. The paper is organised around two main questions: whether locality-aware hierarchical compression is genuinely supported by the data, and whether the disentangling layers of MERA contribute beyond a simpler tree hierarchy. To address these questions, we combine benchmark comparisons with a training-free local-compressibility diagnostic and a direct identity-disentangler ablation. In the nominal benchmark, the MERA-inspired model attains a higher mean AUC than the dense autoencoder at all three latent dimensions while using roughly one-third of its trainable parameters. The locality-preserving multiscale structure is well matched to jet data, and, at the strongest compression bottleneck, the trained disentanglers move substantially away from the identity and are accompanied by a positive mean performance shift. Overall, the study supports locality-aware hierarchical compression as a useful and parameter-efficient inductive bias for reconstruction-based jet anomaly detection in this benchmark setting.

Machine Learning.title: Attention to Mamba: A Recipe for Cross-Architecture Distillation
Machine Learning.summary:
arXiv:2604.14191v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: State Space Models (SSMs) such as Mamba have become a popular alternative to Transformer models, due to their reduced memory consumption and higher throughput at generation compared to their Attention-based counterparts. On the other hand, the community has built up a considerable body of knowledge on how to train Transformers, and many pretrained Transformer models are readily available. To facilitate the adoption of SSMs while leveraging existing pretrained Transformers, we aim to identify an effective recipe to distill an Attention-based model into a Mamba-like architecture. In prior work on cross-architecture distillation, however, it has been shown that a na\"ive distillation procedure from Transformers to Mamba fails to preserve the original teacher performance, a limitation often overcome with hybrid solutions combining Attention and SSM blocks. The key argument from our work is that, by equipping Mamba with a principled initialization, we can recover an overall better recipe for cross-architectural distillation. To this end, we propose a principled two-stage approach: first, we distill knowledge from a traditional Transformer into a linearized version of Attention, using an adaptation of the kernel trick. Then, we distill the linearized version into an adapted Mamba model that does not use any Attention block. Overall, the distilled Mamba model retains most of the original Pythia-1B Transformer performance, reaching a perplexity of 14.01 close to the teacher's 13.86. This largely carries over to downstream tasks, although some gaps appear on tasks relying more on in-context recall. To show the efficacy of our recipe, we conduct thorough ablations at 1B scale with 10B tokens varying sequence mixer architecture, scaling analysis on model sizes and total distillation tokens, and a sensitivity analysis on tokens allocation between stages.

Machine Learning.title: Medial Axis Aware Learning of Signed Distance Functions
Machine Learning.summary:
arXiv:2604.16512v3 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: We propose a novel variational method to compute a highly accurate global signed distance function (SDF) to a given point cloud. To this end, the jump set of the gradient of the SDF, which coincides with the medial axis of the surface, is explicitly taken into account through a higher-order variational formulation that enforces linear growth along the gradient direction away from this discontinuity set. The eikonal equation and the zero-level set of the SDF are enforced as constraints. To make this variational problem computationally tractable, a phase field approximation of Ambrosio-Tortorelli type is employed. The associated phase field function implicitly describes the medial axis. The method is implemented for surfaces represented by unoriented point clouds using neural network approximations of both the SDF and the phase field. Experiments demonstrate the method's accuracy both in the near field and globally. Quantitative and qualitative comparisons with other approaches show the advantages of the proposed method.

Machine Learning.title: Estimating Implicit Regularization in Deep Learning
Machine Learning.summary:
arXiv:2605.05436v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Deep learning systems are known to exhibit implicit regularization (alt. implicit bias), favoring simple solutions instead of merely minimizing the loss function. In some cases, we can analytically derive the implicit regularization -- connecting it to an equivalent penalty that augments the learning objective. However, modern deep learning systems are complex, carrying modifications to the training procedure and architecture (e.g. early stopping, minibatching, dropout) whose effects are not always directly interpretable. Although estimating the resulting implicit regularization could aid theorists in algorithm design and practitioners in interpreting their hyperparameter choices, this problem has received little direct attention. It is also tractable: regularization makes weight updates deviate from loss gradients, promising a signal for identifying implicit bias. Here we provide gradient matching methods that can be used to empirically estimate the implicit regularization. Our method works on networks with known regularization, recovering popular explicit penalties like $\ell_1$ and $\ell_2$. It also replicates known implicit effects, like the quadratic weight penalty induced by early stopping in gradient descent, demonstrating that it can be used to test theories of implicit regularization. Crucially, because our method is empirical, it can handle implicit regularization in arbitrary networks. We demonstrate this use by characterizing implicit $\ell_2$ effects of dropout in deep networks. Our work shows that practitioners can use gradient matching to understand regularization in networks with implicit biases that are too complicated to derive analytically.

Machine Learning.title: Structural Rationale Distillation via Reasoning Space Compression
Machine Learning.summary:
arXiv:2605.07139v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: When distilling reasoning from large language models (LLMs) into smaller ones, teacher rationales for similar problems often vary wildly in structure and strategy. Like a chef who makes the same dish differently each time, this inconsistency burdens the student with noisy supervision that is hard to internalize. We propose Distillation through Reasoning Path Compression (D-RPC), which constrains the teacher to follow a compact, dynamically maintained bank of reusable high-level reasoning paths. For each training question, D-RPC retrieves the most relevant path and conditions the teacher to follow it, producing rationales that are consistent across similar problems yet diverse enough to cover different problem types. A PAC-Bayes analysis formalizes a trade-off between bank size and coverage, with smaller banks limiting path diversity at the risk of coverage gaps. Our ablations favor an intermediate bank size, consistent with this trade-off. Across five math and commonsense reasoning benchmarks with two student models, D-RPC achieves the highest average accuracy among the evaluated distillation methods, while using fewer tokens than template-heavy alternatives.

Machine Learning.title: Factual recall in linear associative memories: sharp asymptotics and mechanistic insights
Machine Learning.summary:
arXiv:2605.10795v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Large language models excel at factual recall, yet the fundamental limits of storing input--output associations with neural networks remain unclear. We study these limits in a minimal setting: a linear associative memory that maps $p$ input embeddings in $\mathbb{R}^d$ to their $d$-dimensional targets via a linear layer, requiring each mapped input to score its own target above all other outputs. Since all inputs compete for the same outputs, these constraints are strongly correlated, which makes the storage capacity $p_c$ --- the largest number of associations that can be stored --- hard to characterise. We address this in three steps. First, we introduce a decoupled model, in which each input competes with its own independent set of outputs, and provide numerical and analytical evidence that it is equivalent to the original model, both in capacity and in the structure of the learnt solution. Second, using tools from statistical physics, we show that the decoupled model has capacity $p_c \log p_c / d^2 = 1/2$, extend this computation to linear two-layer networks, and go beyond the capacity by predicting the spectrum of the learnt weights and the storage mechanism. The latter explains how the optimal solution outperforms a na\"ive Hebbian rule: rather than boosting input--output alignments with broad fluctuations, it raises the correct scores just above the extreme-value threshold set by the competing outputs. Third, we prove the decoupled model's capacity thresholds rigorously, including in the non-convex two-layer case; combined with a recent proof for the original model, this shows that both models have the same capacity for full-rank weights. These findings give a sharp characterisation of factual storage in linear networks, and suggest decoupling as a general tool for memorisation and learning problems in which each input must be matched to one of an extensive number of outputs.

Machine Learning.title: Agentic Literature Extraction Augments Targeted Protein Degradation Databases
Machine Learning.summary:
arXiv:2605.11221v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Predictive models in medicinal chemistry depend on structured assay data locked in primary publications. This bottleneck is acute in targeted protein degradation (TPD), where each assay record must combine compound identity, degradation target, recruiter, assay context, and endpoint values reported across sections, tables, and supplementary files. Existing TPD databases are manually curated and often lack assay context. We present an expert-in-the-loop large language model workflow in which a cross-validated prompt-refinement module adapts extraction instructions from scarce expert annotations. With only seven annotated molecular glue publications, the workflow achieved record-level $F_1 = 0.98$ and transferred to proteolysis-targeting chimeras (PROTACs) by terminology substitution alone ($F_1 \geq 0.93$). The resulting database, AutoTPD, contained 81% and 92% more molecular glue and PROTAC records than standardized reference datasets; expert audits found 92/100 and 33/40 new records to be correct. Applying the workflow to eligible PubMed Central open-access literature added 4,483 records from 598 publications, yielding AutoTPD+, a public, versioned database of 7,622 TPD records, including degradation assay measurements, designed for monthly updates. In a controlled surrogate model comparison, PROTAC degradation activity models trained on AutoTPD+ saw a 8.9-18.2% error reduction relative to models trained on the original PROTAC-DB data.

Machine Learning.title: EPIC: Efficient Predicate-Guided Inference-Time Control for Compositional Text-to-Image Generation
Machine Learning.summary:
arXiv:2605.11722v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Recent text-to-image (T2I) generators can synthesize realistic images, but still struggle with compositional prompts involving multiple objects, counts, attributes, and relations.
